Australia’s first joint space unit, the No. 1 Space Surveillance Unit (1SSU), began operations in January 2023 and is in charge of the C-band radar and the SST.14 The Australian Defence Force (ADF)’s Space Command held Exercise Pitch Black 24 in August 2024 to strengthen its SSA capabilities.15 This was completed through partnership with the US Space Force’s Joint Commercial Operations (JCO) network, which is striving to provide 24 hour space surveillance.16 This exercise consisted of the following actors: ADF, New Zealand Defence Force, Japan Air Self-Defense Force, and the Australian Bureau of Meteorology.17 Chief of Joint Capabilities Lieutenant General Susan Coyle said, “Investment in space capabilities that enhance intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance is a top priority under our National Defence Strategy.” 18 In January 2026, Australia’s DoD announced a $2.9 million AUS contract with Space Machines to create a threat detection system, Space Threat Analysis and Response System (STARS).19 This 24 month-long project aims to create technology capable of ingesting data from ground-based SSA systems, along with commercial providers, in order to predict RPOs, close fly-bys, or other potential sources of interference to Australian and allies’ satellites in LEO. Following the completion of this project, the Space Machines Company plans to incorporate this capability into their Solstice OS system, which Australia plans to eventually offer allies access to.20 The STARS project is intended to strengthen Australian SSA capabilities, through integration into command and control systems, with the goal of streamlining spacecraft fleet operations and on-demand orbital services.21 ***Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability (DARC) Program*** In December 2023, the United States announced that Australia and the United Kingdom had officially joined the Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability (DARC) program.22 DARC is an effort to develop a new set of radars to detect, track, and identify objects in deep space and consists of three geographically distributed sites that each have multiple transmit and receive radars meshed together (see US Space Situational Awareness Capabilities, Section 1.5). Australia was assigned the first operational site, “Site 1.” 23 In September 2022, Northrop Grumman was awarded the contract to build Site 1 in Western Australia and began this work in October 2023; the first of twenty-seven antennas was completed in February 2024.24

06-02

DARC has been having issues maintaining its set schedule. USSF’s Gen. Stephen Purdy said in February 2025 that DARC might be one of the “slow” and “expensive” legacy systems that might be better replaced by commercial providers.25 A June 2025 report by the US Government Accountability Office (GAO) noted that delays in the build of Site 1 because of issues in creating the site’s systems integration lab were “due to the contractor’s lack of expertise in building such a lab” and that seven-month delay had created follow-on delays.26 For example, “the program delayed Site 2 construction by 9 months to April 2027 and deferred operational acceptance by 13 months to November

2029. Similarly, for Site 3, the program postponed both construction start and operational acceptance by 26 months, to September 2029 and January 2032, respectively.” 27 In August 2025, Northrop Grumman reported that Site 1’s “calibrated antenna arrays operated as a single system to successfully characterize the movement of multiple satellites and demonstrate the effectiveness of the system’s precision radar tracking technology” and is scheduled to be completed in 2027.28 Despite delays in the sites’ construction, the entire DARC system is still scheduled to be operational by 2032.29
**6.3 — AUSTRALIAN COUNTERSPACE POLICY, DOCTRINE,** **AND ORGANIZATION** In the July 2020 *Defence Strategic Update*, the Australian government identified several key issue areas it wanted to focus on in space. These include assured access to space, a satellite network to allow for independent communications, SSA capabilities (sensors and tracking), and “an enhanced space control program.” On the same day, Australia’s *Force Structure Plan 2020* included a chapter on the space domain, and noted that “Continued investment and development of space capabilities will be required to further improve Defence’s resilience and enhance a large number of space-dependent capabilities across the Joint Force.” In the section about space control, it calls for a focus on space domain awareness but also notes that its plans include “the development of options to enhance ADF space control through capabilities to counter emerging space threats to Australia’s free use of the space domain and that assure our continued access to space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance.” Australia’s DoD was reported to have been undertaking a “space domain review” as part of its efforts to recognize space as a full operational warfighting domain. It was intended to be completed in March 2023, but as of February 2026, it is not known to have been completed. Australia announced in May 2021 that it would be establishing an ADF space command that will be housed within the RAAF. It is intended to bring together the three branches of the Australian military with representatives of the Australian government with the goal of creating “an organisation to sustain, force-generate, operate space capabilities, and assign them to a joint operation command if needed.” 30 Air Marshall Mel Hupfeld, chief of the Australian Air Force, clarified that while there were concerns about space being contested, “this does not mean that defence encourages the militarisation of space,” and that “All space operations are conducted consistent with international and domestic legal obligations.” 31 In March 2022, Air Vice-Marshal Catherine Roberts, the head of the ADF’s new space command, stated, “I think the activities by China and Russia, which have been fairly well documented in the public domain, scare me… We need to accelerate the capabilities so we can deal with

the threats.” The space command, officially established in March 2022 with about 100 personnel, is reported to be investigating irreversible and reversible ways in which to disable enemy satellites (via lasers or jamming) but will not use counterspace capabilities that create debris.33 In March 2022, Australia announced the head of its space agency had begun working on a national space strategy, its “Space Strategic Update” (SSU), which was intended to guide the country’s space activities and priorities to the 2040s and integrate its military, commercial, and civil space efforts.34 It was intended to take 18 months to be completed.35 Australia’s SSU was renamed to the *National Space Policy* in 2022,36 but the report has not been published as of February 2026. Australian Industry and Science Minister Ed Husic stated in March 2023 that he did not intend to “automatically” progress work on the *National Space Policy*, as the project was announced by the former Australian government.37 In August 2024, Australian Senator David Fawcett noted that $9.5 million had been committed toward the development of this report.38 Australia’s Department of Defence intends to invest $7 billion AUD in space over the next decade.39 This was announced in July 2020 as part of its 2020 *Defence Strategic Update and 2020 Force Structure Plan* and is planned to be used on developing space services and emerging space technologies.40 Also in March 2022, Australia released its *Defence Space Strategy*, reaffirming its $7 billion AUD planned to be spent on space capabilities by 2036. The strategy declared that the mission of the Australian military forces in space was to shape the space domain, deter competitor actions, and respond as necessary to assure access to space capabilities. The document lists five “lines of effort” to meet that vision:

- “Enhance space capability to assure Joint Force access in a congested, contested and competitive space environment;
- “Deliver military effects integrated across Whole of Government and with allies and partners in support of Australia’s national security;
- “Increase the national understanding of the criticality of space;
- “Advance Australian sovereign space capability to support the development of a sustainable national space enterprise; and
- “Evolve the Defence Space Enterprise to ensure a coherent, efficient and effective use of the space domain.” 41
The strategy also discussed Department of Defence’s role in continuing to “identify Space Control gaps and opportunities to develop a credible Space Control capability, and space capability developers will actively seek to improve resilience of the space capabilities,” noting as well, “Defence will explore options consistent with its commitment to be a responsible actor in space.” In March 2022, Australia’s Defence Space Command released a *Space Power* *eManual*.42It describes itself as “the foundational Defence reference on the employment of space power, complementing and supporting all levels of Defence education and doctrine,” and space power is further defined as “the total strength of a nation’s ability to conduct and influence activities to, in, through and from space to achieve its objectives.” 43 Space control is described as involving “offensive and defensive operations to ensure freedom of action in space by defeating efforts to interfere with or attack Australian or allied space systems and, when directed, deny space services to a competitor,” and that those activities may happen in any operating domain, and is made up of “offensive space control, defensive space control, space electronic warfare and the aspects of navigation warfare that deal with space based PNT.” 06-04

In October 2022, Australia formally pledged not to conduct destructive DA-ASAT missile tests, as one of the growing number of signatories to the moratorium on such testing initiated by the United States. In April 2023, Australia released the public version of its *Defence Strategic* *Review* (DSR), which is a periodic assessment of defense capabilities and status that has only been done twice previously (in 1986 and 2012).46 The review was prompted by recent changes in the strategic environment, largely driven by the continued rise of China, and political dissatisfaction with how previous Australian defense policy addressed emerging challenges. This 2023 review included significant attention to space as a new domain of operations and recommended moving space into the Joint Capabilities Group (JCG), creating a centralized development and management function for space, and building a career path for space professionals.47 The Australian Department of Defence manages the JCG, along with components of their work including cyber operations and satellite communications.48 The Australian Department of Defence revealed multiple initiatives in July 2023, focused on increasing their space defense capabilities and lining up with key components of the 2023 DSR.49 One of these included the Defence Space Command’s transfer to the RAAF, along with the creation of the ADF’s first joint space unit.50 According to Lieutenant General John Frewen, Chief of Joint Capabilities, the DSR focused on the importance of better coordination between space, cyber, and information warfare.51 Australia’s Department of Defence intends to invest in AUD $9-12 billion in space over the next decade.52 This was announced in April 2024 as part of its *2024 Defence Integrated Investment Plan*, which was jointly released with the *2024 National Defence Strategy*. The 2024 Integrated Investment Program is expected to focus on resilient communications, surveillance, reconnaissance, and space domain awareness.53 The Australian DoD is currently updating their *2024 National Defence Strategy*, aiming to publish this update sometime in

2026.54 Australian officials in October 2025 spoke about their interest in developing space control capabilities, citing their space operations framework, concept SELENE.55 While that concept is not available online, Australian military writing has discussed it, including stating what is described to be its core tenant, “The ADF will seek space advantage to enable freedom of action by temporally assuring access and disrupting or denying an adversary use of the space domain, as required.” 56 Australia participated in US Space Command’s exercise Global Sentinel 2025 in April 2025 (See US Counterspace Policy, Doctrine, and Organization, Section

“Space Operations Specialist.” According to Australian Defence Personnel Minister Matt Keogh, this was to “grow the ADF’s capabilities in space operations” and is a step s in building “Australians sovereign space workforce,” which will eventually include positions focusing on missile warning, space control, and space surveillance.62 **Potential Military Utility /** Australia has made significant policy changes aimed at developing more of a national security space capability and dealing with space threats. Between creating a project to develop a ground-based EW counterspace capability and statements from Australian military officials about the importance of Australia developing that capability, it is likely that Australia will have at least an initial EW counterspace capability in the near future. Furthermore, given the amount of policy documents being generated for defense space purposes, it would appear that Australia is serious about having the option to use its nascent EW counterspace capability, so it is most likely going to be operational in some capacity. Additionally, given the investment in its SSA capabilities and physical possession of some SSA radars already, should Australia decide to target space assets for offensive measures, it is likely to have at least some inherent capacity to do so.

# F R ANC E

2.3522°E

While France has long had a civil space program, as well as military satellites, it was not until recently that France had an explicit focus on offensive and defensive counterspace activities. The major change occurred in July 2019 with the release of the first French Space Defense Strategy, which elevated French military space efforts and control of French military satellites. While some French officials initially suggested machine guns on satellites, the actual plan calls for ground-based lasers for dazzling and satellites equipped for on-orbit inspections and also with lasers used for what has been described as self- defense, but could suggest the potential for enabling counterspace capability. Subsequently, new demonstration assets are slated for deployment, including “patrol-guard” satellites and in-orbit lasers. Since 2021, France has carried out annual military exercises, codenamed “ASTERX,” in outer space, testing the capabilities of its Space Command, as part of France’s evolving goal to be the world’s third-largest spatial power.1 France and the United States conducted two RPO engagements in 2025.

**7.1 — FRENCH CO-ORBITAL ASATs** In July 2019, when announcing France’s interest in developing active coun- terspace capabilities, French Minister of Defense Florence Parly reportedly offered the option of including machine guns on satellites that would theoret- ically target enemy satellites’ solar panels. This was part of a larger discussion about how “our allies and adversaries are militarising space... we need to act.”3 However, in private discussions with French officials, this was clarified as having been a poorly-used metaphor. Orbital mechanics severely limits the utility of projectile weapons in orbit. In the context of Operation ARES (Action et RÉsilience Spatiale), France has started the development of demonstration assets in GEO and LEO, to prepare the deployment of the Engin géodérivant d’intervention et de découragement (Geosynchronous Drift Intervention and Deterrence Vehicle, EGIDE) program to produce operational patrol satellites.4 To support this initiative, new demonstration assets are planned to be de- ployed, including the programming of patrol-guard satellites (Yeux en Orbite pour un Démonstrateur Agile, or YODA) and in-orbit lasers (FLAMHE project).5 These experiments will be complemented by the TOUTATIS (In-Orbit Test of Action Techniques against Attempted Spatial Interference) program that aims to implement a comprehensive chain of knowledge and response to attempt- ed space interference.6 These YODA satellites are intended to be launched to GEO in 2026 or 2027, provided a launch slot is found, and are intended to be an RPO surveillance or inspection platform, similar to the United States’ GSSAP program (see US Co-Orbital ASAT, Section 1.1). The YODA program is7 also framed as an early technology demonstrator program of later and bigger versions of inspector satellites that would be able to protect French military satellites by 2030.8 In parallel with this program, the use of in-orbit laser technologies (FLAMHE project) is being considered as non-kinetic means to neutralize unfriendly satellites without creating any debris.9

In September 2024, French Space Command leader Major General Philippe Adam, and company executives from U-SPACE and MBDA kicked off a demonstration program aiming to provide France with active space defense capabilities.11 This will start with TOUTATIS, a LEO demonstration, that aims to complement the experiments that will be carried out in geostationary orbit by the YODA satellites. As the first building block of the ARES operation, led by the French Procurement agency (Direction générale de l’armement), the TOUTATIS experiment involves two demonstration nanosatellites.12 SPLINTER, a “low-orbit action” satellite, will have a high maneuvering capability and a set of subsystems enabling autonomous approach and actions. LISA-1, a “spotter” satellite, will be deployed to provide enhanced observation capabilities for space surveillance from orbit.13 Carried out by U-SPACE, in partnership with MBDA, the TOUTATIS experiment is intended to start in 2026.14 While announcing a major increase in French military space spending, President Emmanuel Macron said in November 2025, “[W]e will deploy our first patrol satellites… starting in 2027 to monitor, inspect, and, if necessary, counter threats in orbit. These will be complemented by our first space-based action capabilities based on lasers and jammers.” 15 The French Defense Innovation Agency is launching a preliminary study named “Salazar” to simulate the capture of dangerous space objects in LEO using a set of numerical models and missions. In November 2024, this study was awarded to the French start-up Dark to prove the feasibility of using a multi-stage space access system, capable of rapidly reaching a specific point in orbit, while bypassing meteorological constraints and certain types of orbital transfer. Its final stage is equipped with a robotic module dedicated to target capture.16 Founded in 2021, Dark developed an interceptor system and announced in July 2024 the completion of the first test campaign of its Sheitan rocket engine that would power its Interceptor vehicle, before a first demonstration of orbital defence capabilities by 2026.17 As part of the Salazar preliminary study, the Defense Innovation Agency was going to supply to Dark a fictitious target equipped with evasion or warning systems, which in turn would present several 07-02

possible scenarios. During the simulation, Dark was supposed to propose the best interception scenario, based on a target’s orbital parameters, taking into account mission strategy, performance and timing. However, in October 2025, Dark closed; it is unclear as to who will continue the Salazar study.19 French interest in possessing their own spaceplane has grown in recent years.20 Figures like French MP Bastien Lachaud stated that, “France cannot afford to fall behind in this field, at the risk of having to buy an off-the-shelf solution or fracking technological relegation.” 21 Additionally, Major General Philippe Koffi, DGA’s Air, Land, and Naval Combat Lead, stated, “A spaceplane is maneuver- able, reusable and flexible, so it can deliver payload in orbit, recover critical assets, conduct reconnaissance and intervene against threats in orbit… (spaceplanes) could deploy satellites, sensors, and even weapons in orbit with- in hours or days and not months…(and offer) rapid transportation, spacecraft servicing, and even recovery of critical assets.” 22 In May 2025, French compa- ny AndroMach received a Centre national d’études spatiales (CNES) contract to test Banger v1 rocket engines, emphasizing the importance of testing the propane-fueled engine, evaluating its thermodynamic performance, which could contribute to eventual French spaceplane technology.23 The follow- ing June, a contract between DGA and Dassault Aviation was announced to develop Véhicule Orbital Réutilisable de Transport et d’Exploration (Reusable Orbital Transport and Exploration Vehicle, VORTEX), a spaceplane demonstra- tor.24 VORTEX is scheduled to be launched on a small rocket in 2028, aiming to validate key technologies and perform atmospheric reentry.25 France and the United States held their first bilateral RPO engagement in April 2025, which involved a US and a French military satellite approaching each other near a “strategic competitors” spacecraft; it is unclear which country that spacecraft belonged to.26 In September 2025, a USSF official said that France and the United States would be engaging in a second RPO mission.27 This ended up happening as part of Operation Olympic Defender in November

2025.28 While both countries acknowledged the maneuvers, they did not provide specifics. However, US commercial SSA company COMSPOC monitored the RPOs and identified the participating satellites as USA 324 (2022-006A, 51280, part of the United States’ GSSAP program) and France’s SYRACUSE 3A (2005-041B, 28885); there were three sets of maneuvers observed (November 11-14, November 22-23, and November 28-29), and, according to a COMSPOC spokesperson, “In all these movements, SYRACUSE 3A seems to lead and USA 324 seems to follow as the maneuvers performed by USA 324 is lagged by a day.” 29The closest the two satellites got to each other was just a little over 25 km.30
**7.2 — FRENCH DIRECT-ASCENT ASATs** There are no known plans for France to have a DA-ASAT capability. France does have a jointly fielded missile defense system with Italy called Surface- to-Air Missile Platform/Terrain (SAMP/T); however, its interception altitude is at best 120 km and is thus not of much military utility as an ASAT weapon.31 France maintains significant expertise in space launch vehicle and ballistic missile technology that could be the basis for a future DA-ASAT program.
**7.3 — FRENCH ELECTRONIC WARFARE** While France has terrestrial-based EW capabilities, there are scant details available in the public domain and it is unclear how effective or operational

French officials have also expressed their willingness to share technology on counterspace EW capabilities with Saudi Arabia, but there has been no public concrete action announced in this area. French authorities have also discovered multiple Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) jammers operating near the Merville airport in March 2023, operated by unknown entities.33 During his hearing on the 2025 Finance Bill, Air Force General Jérôme Bellanger declared that France is “continuing to study jamming” technologies.34

**7.4 — FRENCH DIRECTED ENERGY WEAPONS** In July 2019, French Minister of Defense Florence Parly indicated the potential for placing lasers on satellites with the goal of protecting them from attack, saying, “If our satellites are threatened, we intend to blind those of our adversaries… We reserve the right and the means to be able to respond: that could imply the use of powerful lasers deployed from our satellites or from patrolling nano-satellites.” 35 These lasers would “dazzle those who would be tempted to approach too close.” 36 At the time of her statement, the plan was to have the first capabilities ready by 2025 with the completion being achieved by 2030, yet this timeline no longer appears to be accurate.37 Further information about these efforts was revealed in April 2023 as part of the French military programming law for 2024-2030. One of the initiatives is BLOOMLASE, a program to develop ground-based lasers used from the ground to dazzle an observation satellite. 38 Another initiative is FLAMHE, a project aiming to develop space-based capabilities to neutralise in-orbit satellites using directed energy weapons. The technology is currently being developed by companies, including ArianeGroup, and is intended to eventually provide France with an operational capability.39 The French Navy’s Chief of Staff stated in front of the French National Assembly that “lasers can also be used as a space warfare weapon operated from boats: they can blind observation satellites to ensure the concealment of naval forces in conflict situations.” 40 France has also conducted tests of the effectiveness of existing ground-based lasers against their Spot remote sensing satellites in LEO.41 When addressing the Commission de la Défense nationale et des Forces Armées (National Defence and Armed Forces Committee) on the 2025 Finance Bill, Air Force General Jérôme Bellanger, Chief of Staff of the Armée de l’air et de l’espace (French Air and Space Force), stated that France is studying directed-energy laser technologies.42 The French Defence Procurement Agency (DGA) is reported to be working on ground-based lasers as part of its anti-drone and area defense laser program, Syderal (Système Laser de Défense de Nouvelle Génération or New Generation Laser Defence System); this system is planned to result in a 50kW laser by 2030 that could be used against satellites as well.43 It is unclear whether these are meant to be destructive laser weapons or those used as countermeasures against the targeting systems of an attacker. A nanosatellite is very unlikely to have sufficient on-board power to generate a destructive laser, although it may be possible to have lower power directed energy systems that could be used to blind, dazzle, or confuse electro-optical targeting systems of approaching co-orbital ASATs or inspection satellites. These systems could operate in a similar manner to the directional infrared countermeasures systems mounted on some modern aircraft to confuse or jam infrared seekers on anti-aircraft missiles. However, successfully aiming such a laser at an approaching satellite or interceptor is a non-trivial challenge.

**7.5 — FRENCH SPACE SITUATIONAL AWARENESS CAPABILITIES** France’s Space Command (CDE) is charged with coordinating SSA for the country as a whole. It operates the Grand Réseau Adapté à la Veille Spatiale (Large Network Adapted for Space Surveillance, GRAVES) radar (see Imagery Appendix, p. 17-53 and p. 17-54), which can see objects with radar cross sections, initially down to 1 meter at an altitude of 400-1000 km.44 Following two major upgrades, the GRAVES radar monitors objects in low Earth orbit, from 200 to 2000 km from three sites in France: the transmission center near Dijon, the reception center near Orange, and the operations center, which opened in Toulouse in June 2024. The system can detect and determine the orbits of satellites crossing its coverage zone 24/7.45 France also has three Système d’Acquisition et de Trajectographie des Avions et des Munitions (SAT- AM) C-band radars that are not primarily SSA sensors but do have a secondary mission to track space debris.46 Another asset which contributes to French SSA capabilities (but does so in the capacity of it being its secondary mission) is the Bâtiment d’Essais et de Mesures (BEM) Monge tracking ship.47 France also has the Système Probatoire d’Observation du Ciel (Experimental Earth Observation System, SPOC) telescope, which can do initial orbit determinations, and the Télescope à Action Rapide pour les Objets Transitoires (TAROT) system of two 25-centimeter telescopes located at the Calern Observatory (see Imagery Appendix, pg 17-55) and an 18 cm telescope at the Les Makes Observatory, which, along with the Radiometry for Ocean colour Satellites Calibration and Community Engagement (ROSACE) telescope, can track objects at GEO.48 All of these capabilities contribute to France’s Centre Opérationnel de Surveillance Militaire des Objets Spatiaux (COSMOS), its Operational Center for Military Surveillance of Space Objects.49 COSMOS operators visited the US 18th Space Defense Squadron, which is charged with running the USSF’s space situational awareness mission, in October 2022 as part of an exchange to improve SSA data sharing and operational best practices.50 France participates in and hosts NATO’s Space Centre of Excellence, which was created in July 2023 and reached full operational status in January 2026.51 According to NATO, the Centre-which is based in Toulouse - “develops space operations concepts, strengthens staff readiness, supports major exercises, and feeds operational lessons back into NATO’s adaptation cycle.” 52 In her July 2019 announcement about France’s interest in counterspace capabilities, French Minister of Defense Florence Parly noted that while France has some existing SSA capabilities, it wished to work with other European Union countries on shoring those up. She specifically said, “France has her independence and is attached to it. But she does not want to be isolated in this new zone of conflicts… I am counting particularly on Germany to become the beating heart of surveillance in space.” 53 The Franco-German Space and Defence Council in 2017 approved a joint SSA project, which is hoped to be able to provide clarifying information about unfriendly or hostile actions in space.54 Minister Parly also said that they plan to use Ariane Group’s Geotracker network in order to capture pictures of objects in GEO.55 During discussions in the Commission de la Défense Nationale et des Forces Armées (National Defence and Armed Forces Committee) on the Draft Budget Bill for 2025, it was pointed out that the law’s priority is to develop the successor to the GRAVES space surveillance radar, with a view to its entry into service as of 2030. A single GRAVES-Next Generation space surveillance radar has been included in the programming law, but has not yet been developed. military communications satellites, which could alert satellites to oncoming threats so that the satellites can take defensive actions or maneuvers. A strategy of maintaining competitiveness and autonomy internationally in the SSA domain is also being pursued by the European Union Space Surveillance and Tracking (EU SST), of which France is a prominent member. The EU SST increased the budget contracted to European Industry in R&D and capabilities by 205 percent in 2020-2022 compared to the 2018-2019 budget.58 In February 2024, the European Health and Digital Executive Agency completed a set of grant agreements under the Horizon Europe projects to support research and development for EU SST services.59 The total budget made available by the EU for the five projects is €52 million for the 2023-2025 period.60 In September 2024, the network of sensors contributing to EU SST has started growing with the integration of new commercial sensors, result- ing from a public procurement procedure led by the CNES for the acquisition of commercial data for a total maximum amount of €13.2 million that was launched in 2023.61 The new sensors aim to enhance the provision of the EU SST services, such as collision avoidance, re-entry analysis, and fragmentation analysis.62 In January 2023, it was announced that the European Defence Fund had awarded a contract to a consortium for the creation of a satellite, Naucrates, that could be placed in GEO in order to do close approaches to other spacecraft there and take centimeter-level resolution images.63 Described as a “Microsatellite for Geostationary Orbit Surveillance and Intelligence” with less than 100 kg mass, the estimated cost for the design and demonstration of the project amounts to around €5 million.64 Naucrates should have a lifespan of 3 to 5 years.65 Celestia TTI, one of the firms involved in the project, announced in April 2024 that the initiative had successfully cleared its critical design review and is on track for delivery by the end of 2025.66 Presumably France, as a member of the European Commission, could get access to the SSA data generated by this satellite. In April 2023, CNES announced that it had selected a consortium led by ArianeGroup to develop a network of ground telescopes and a space- based sensor to augment its existing SSA capabilities.67 As of February 2026, there have been no updates on their progress.

07-06

The French military programming law for 2024-2030 includes the creation, by 2028, of an operational command and control capability of space operations named “Astreos”, based on the capabilities of a high-performance computer adapted to the massive processing of space surveillance data, as part of Operation ARES.68 French company Infinite Orbits won a contract from France’s Directorate General of Armament in August 2025 for the €50M (Positioning and Autonomous Laser Assisted Detection in Near-space) PALADIN framework agreement, which is a part of the ARES program.69 Infinite Orbits will be responsible for the creation of a GEO inspection and monitoring service for the French Space Command, which includes a desired launch date of 2027.70 It is intended to be able to get within 1 km of other satellites.71 In 2011, France and the United States reached an agreement to exchange information on space debris in orbit, with the aim of strengthening the protection of satellites operated by their respective armed forces.72 In 2020, France and Germany joined the Combined Space Operations (CSpO) initiative to develop coordination and interoperability of their efforts, increase resilience and encourage responsible behavior in outer space.73 After having rejected in 2021 a first offer to join,74 France joined the Multinational Force Operation Olympic Defender (MNF-OOD) in October 2024, an initiative launched in 2013 by the United States to foster international cooperation in space defense.75 MNF-OOD aims to optimize space operations, build resilience in space systems, synchronize efforts to strengthen deterrence against hostile actors, and reduce the spread of on-orbit debris. Participants commit to improve data and information sharing, contribute to the deterrence of competitors and create a common operational culture in outer space, by refining their understanding of the space environment, including the training of national operators. DGA issued a contract as part of the ARES program to Thales in October 2025 to develop, deliver, and deploy the ground-based LEO space surveillance radar system, AURORE.76 AURORE will provide uninterrupted monitoring and tracking of multiple objects at the same time, through a software-defined radar system within an Ultra High Frequency (UHF) band.77

**7.6 — FRENCH COUNTERSPACE POLICY, DOCTRINE, AND ORGANIZATION** In September 2018, Parly surprised some by openly calling out the Russians for using their Luch Olymp satellite to allegedly attempt to spy on France’s Athena- Fidus satellite (2014-006B, 39509) (see Russian Co-Orbital ASAT, Section 2.1). She said, “It got so close that we might have imagined it was trying to intercept our communications,” and commented, “Trying to listen to your neighbors is not only unfriendly. It’s an act of espionage.” 78 It should be noted that surveillance of this type does not violate any existing international laws.

In July 2019, French President Emmanuel Macron announced that by September 1 of that year, France would be elevating the existing Joint Space Command within the French Air Force to be a full Space Command and renaming the French Air Force to be the Air and Space Force, or the Armée de l’Air et de l’Espace. He said that this was to, “ensure the development and reinforcement of our space capabilities.” 79 France’s Space Command or Commandement de l’espace (CDE) is starting off with 220 people as its staff and will grow eventually to 500 when it reaches full operational capacity in 2030.80 According to Parly, “Eventually, this command will be responsible for all our space operations, under the orders of the Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces.” She noted the importance of the Ministry of Armed Forces becoming a space operator, as “If we want to be able to carry out real military space operations, we must develop autonomy of action.” 81 CDE moved in November its offices to Toulouse to be co-located, near CNES, France’s civil space agency.82 The French military had originally put aside €3.6-billion (roughly $4 billion USD) to invest in its satellites from 2019-2025.83 Parly announced in July 2019 an additional €700 million for this effort.84 This €4.3 billion includes funds for refreshing France’s military space infrastructure (reconnaissance, signals intelligence, and communications satellites, as well as the GRAVES radar used for space surveillance). Parly also noted that France will be testing a long-range radar as a result of increased missile threats. In July 2019, France also announced its first *Stratégie Spatiale de Défense (Space* *Defence Strategy)*.85 It has two goals: to increase and strengthen SSA for there to be better decision-making and to protect French and selected European space assets. This strategy is intended to be defensive in nature, with Parly noting in her July 2019 speech that this was “not an arms race.” 86 According to Parly, “active defense is not an offensive strategy, it’s all about self-defense…That is, when a hostile act has been detected, characterized and attributed, to be able to respond in an appropriate and proportionate way, in conformity with the principles of international law.” 87 The *Space Defence Strategy* noted that the renewed doctrine for military space operations will have the following four functions: “support for space capabilities, situational awareness, support for operations and action in space.” 88 It also stated that a “consolidated assessment of threats affecting our capabilities” will be needed.89 The Agence de l’Innovation de Défense (Defense Innovation Agency, AID) is intended to take part in space research and development guidelines. The strategy talks about the need to be able to respond to “unfriendly, illegal or aggressive acts, in accordance with international law.” 90 It gives the following guidelines for responses in these cases:

- In the face of an unfriendly act in space, France reserves the right to take retaliatory measures;
- in response to an unlawful act committed against it, it may take countermeasures with the sole purpose of putting an end to it, in accordance with its obligations under international law; these countermeasures will be strictly necessary and proportionate to the objective;
- in the event of armed aggression in space, France can make use of its right to self-defence.91
The strategy recommends France continue to participate in multilateral fora, especially so it can “focus on behavioural standards to ensure strategic stability

07-08

and avoid opportunities for misunderstandings or escalations.” As part of this overhaul of France’s military space capabilities, the Ministère des Armées would now be allowed to conduct activities in space. To allow for this shift toward military space, France’s National Space Law will have to go through inter- ministerial discussions to be adapted to reflect this new set-up. Published in June 2008, the *Space Operations Act* (LOS) encourages space activity to be primarily commercial and/or civil in nature.93 It was created in order to meet France’s Article VI obligations of the 1967 *Outer Space Treaty*, which requires continuing supervision of national space activities. In February 2022, France’s Space Operations Law was modified to reflect its military space strategy, allowing civilian assets to be transferred to the Ministère des Armées (Ministry of the Armed Forces) designated the Ministère des Armées to be liable if those assets caused any damage, and permitted the Ministère des Armées to commandeer civilian assets.94 ***Stratégie Nationale Spatiale 2025-2040*** France released its new national space policy in November 2025. The *Stratégie* *Nationale Spatiale 2025-2040* consists of “Pillars” and “Strategic Objectives,” which focus on ensuring strategic autonomy, industrial strength, and security in space for the French.95 Pillar 3, “Strengthening the Resilience and Responsiveness of the Military Space Architecture and Accelerate the Deployment of Capabilities in and towards Space,” states as its mission to “Guarantee the security, continuity, and resilience of space infrastructure in a contested, congested, and vulnerable orbit environment, by combining protection, capability autonomy, defensive action, and situational awareness.” 96 Below Pillar 3 are four strategic objectives:

- Strategic Objective 6, “Strengthen the resilience of critical civil and military space infrastructure,” outlines improving resiliency by “redundancy of components (orbital, ground, cyber), diversification of suppliers, use of dual-use solutions, ability to operate in degraded mode, rapid response procedures in the event of failure, etc.”
- Strategic Objective 7, “Guarantee the operational autonomy of sovereign space assets,” details how France plans to improve its freedom of action by focusing on “the sovereignty of space capabilities in three critical areas: intelligence, military telecommunications and early warning.”
- Strategic Objective 8, “Strengthen French and European space surveillance capabilities to ensure autonomous assessment and decision-making in the face of orbital threats,” discusses how France wants to “strengthen the entire SSA chain in order to build a sovereign, precise, reliable, responsive, and resilient SSA capabilities.”
- Strategic Objective 9, “Possess a national capability for active defense in and towards space,” calls for France “to protect and defend national interests, prevent and deter hostile acts, ensure the continuity of strategic missions and, where necessary, act directly in and towards space, while guaranteeing strict compliance with the core principles of the international space law applicable to outer space.” Along these lines, it notes that this depends “on the development of detection, characterisation and attribution capabilities. These capabilities will be complemented by capabilities to disrupt, degrade or even neutralise, if necessary, an adversary’s capabilities, in accordance with international law and based on a logic of gradation and proportionality.” Finally, priority is given to the ground segment of space systems, as it is “the most vulnerable.” 100

and 2025. In 2023, France adopted its military programming law for 2024- 2030, amounting to €400 billion, including €6 billion dedicated to the space domain with a threefold ambition: to increase both the observation and intelligence capabilities and the defense capabilities of satellites.102 In November 2025, while announcing France’s new space strategy, Macron pledged a €4.2 billion investment in military space activities up to 2030, with an eventual investment in space weapons likely to be over €10 billion by 2030.103 While making the announcement, Macron said, “The war of today is already being fought in space, and the war of tomorrow will begin in space… Space is no longer a sanctuary, it has become a battlefield.” 104 In 2021, the Ministère des Armées legally conducted its first military exercises in outer space.105 The exercise was codenamed “ASTERX,” and it tested the capabilities of CDE in tackling 18 different space events and threats to its satellites and defense equipment.106 Since then, ASTERX has been held annually; the 2022 version simulated 16 events and an orbital population of 10,000 objects.107 It was broader in terms of scope from the previous year’s exercise in that it included the European External Action Service (EEAS) plus four other countries; it also incorporated commercial data via the Commercial Integration Cell (CIC).108 The 2023 version proposed 23 space events, including one in the cyber domain,109 and the 2024 version involved 23 events, including 14 different types of threats, ranging from a satellite rendezvous to an attack on a military satellite.110 CDE held the 2025 edition of ASTERX in March, emphasizing various frameworks of cooperation in all domains including space: tactical, strategic, political, and diplomatic.111 This exercise had two phases; the first focused on the French national response to a threat and the second broadened it to international partnerships.112 In November 2022, France formally pledged not to conduct destructive DA-ASAT missile tests, as one of the growing number of signatories to the moratorium on such testing initiated by the United States.113

07-10

In November 2024, French General Philippe Adam, Commander of CDE, pointed out that, faced with the prospect of a conflict in space, the CDE has several missions: to maintain space support for military operations, and to plan and conduct military operations to control space in order to protect satellites up to 36,000 km above Earth.114 Furthermore, speaking to the Commission de la Défense Nationale et des Forces Armées on the Draft Budget Bill for 2025, Air Force General Jérôme Bellanger, Chief of Staff of the French Air Force and Space Ministry, said that France “sticks to an active defense approach, excluding any offensive mindset” and added it “does not develop missiles designed to destroy certain satellites.” 115 The United States started its Schriever Wargame in 1998 as a biennial tabletop exercise to look at how advanced space technologies influenced future conflicts in space. In recent years, the Schriever Wargame has become an annual event that also explored policy and strategy issues, diplomatic, economic, military, and information activities, and included participation from a growing number of allied military and commercial partners. France has been participating in it since 2012.116 The 17th and most recent iteration of the Schriever Wargame was held in August 2025, included policy-makers from Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, New Zealand, Norway, and the United Kingdom, and had an Indo-Pacific focus.117 It included a special access cell so that the participants could share information about special access programs.118 The next version of the wargame will be in 2027 and for the first time, will have allies involved in its creation and planning, as opposed to the United States doing all of it.119 France participated in US Space Command’s Global Sentinel 2025 in April 2025 (See US Counterspace Policy, Doctrine, and Organization, Section 1.6).120 This event included nearly 30 partner nations, including NATO, aiming to strengthen international partnerships, collaboration, and responsible space behaviors.121 The Global Sentinel exercised a dedicated Global Sentinel version of Space- Track.org for capstone modeling and simulation gameplay, replicating potential real world events through this usage.122 Building on this international cooperation, South Korea’s Defense Acquisition Program Administration (DAPA) announced their agreement with the DGA to build upon bilateral defense cooperation in space in September 2025, specifically focusing on research and development and intelligence sharing.123 In October 2025, DGA launched a “Space Pact”, aimed to address space sector challenges through engagement with 50+ companies.124 This is an effort by the Ministère des Armées to align industrial capacity with military requirements and includes other government agencies like CNES and the French Aerospace Lab; it will be carried out with the support of the New Space France Alliance and the French Aerospace Industries Association.125

**Potential Military Utility /** France plans to have inspector satellites deployed by 2027; these satellites could provide France with a co-orbital counterspace capability, even though their stated mission is to defend French satellites. Between the SAMP/T missile defense system and its extensive space launch and ballistic missile expertise, France has the technological building blocks to develop a DA-ASAT capability if it chooses to do so, although there are no indications it has such plans. France is developing the initial capability for ground-based DEW and RPO satellites armed with DEW in both LEO and GEO that may enable a future co-orbital ASAT program, but it is unclear whether they will be capable of just temporary dazzling or doing more permanent damage to other satellites. France’s successful coordination of a bilateral RPO with the United States, along with planning future RPOs, demonstrates its growth in this technology area. Additionally, France’s indigenous SSA capabilities are fairly well-devel- oped so they could potentially be used for targeting non-French satellites and could be of limited military utility as well. Finally, given the amount of policy doc- uments and military space organization being generated for defense space purposes, it would appear that France is serious about using counterspace capabilities, once they are more solidly developed.

07-1 2

52.5186°N

# GERMANY

13.3762°E

Germany historically has had a civil focus to its space program. However, its military, the Bundeswehr, is working to expand its presence in orbit. The combination of a significant planned investment in space and defense systems over the next five years, a new space strategy, and growing engagement in space surveillance points to an increase in German abilities to develop the necessary capabilities to potentially carry out attacks against space systems, should it choose to do so. Germany is changing rapidly from having no offensive counterspace capabilities, to soon having several options available to it.

**8.1 — GERMAN CO-ORBITAL ASATs** Germany currently does not have a co-orbital counterspace capability but it is looking to develop one. Maj. Gen. Michael Traut, commander of the German Space Command, otherwise known as Weltraumkommando der Bundeswehr (WRKdoBw), said in September 2024 that Germany is considering creating a program called “German Inspector Satellite for Multiple Operations,” that could inspect satellites and have arms so it could have the option to respond to threat satellites. Traut talked in May 2025 about having extremely maneuverable1 satellites: “What if we could launch or have some nice little satellites up there, which are agile and go after some satellites which we feel need to be inspected– some sort of space police?” 2 He also said he was “pretty much interested” in interfering with adversaries’ systems.3 In August 2025, the Deutsches Zentrum für Luft-und Raumfahrt or DLR (German Aerospace Center) released requests for information for two types of maneuvering satellites that can conduct close approaches to other spacecraft: one that can be an inspector satellite and one with active defense capabilities.4 The call states that the satellites are to be delivered eleven months after the contracts are signed and that they are to be launched via a “national launcher.” 5 The *Space Safety and Security Strategy* released by Germany in November 2025 calls for developing and using “highly agile low-signal surveillance and bodyguard satellites and reusable spaceplanes.” 6 (For a longer discussion of the strategy, see Section 8.6, German Counterspace Policy, Doctrine, and Organization below.)
**8.2 — GERMAN DIRECT-ASCENT ASATs** In December 2025, Germany received its first Arrow 3 ballistic missile defense battery from Israel; this was a delivery on a $4 billion contract signed in September 2023 between the two countries. Three batteries were originally7 planned for as part of the 2023 deal; the first is based at the Holzdorf military airfield about 40 miles south of Berlin, while eventually the other batteries are intended to be fielded in its northern territory (Schleswig-Holstein), and its southern territory (Bavaria). Shortly after the first battery was delivered,8 Germany and Israel signed an expansion deal worth an additional $3.1 billion USD for more Arrow 3 interceptors and launchers.9 While the exact capabilities of the Arrow 3 in a counterspace role are unknown, it reportedly achieved an exoatmospheric intercept for the first time in November 2023 when it was used to intercept a long-range missile fired from Houthi-controlled Yemen.10 It is unclear at what altitude the intercept was made, only that it was likely above 100 km. The Arrow 3’s range suggests that it can theoretically intercept targets up to 1200 km but its manufacturer, Israeli Aerospace Industries (IAI), estimates that the system is able to intercept

**8.3 — GERMAN ELECTRONIC WARFARE** Maj. Gen. Michael Traut, commander of the German Space Command, told a society of electronic warfare specialists in May 2025, “I would really like to see every future or present space system–not only satellite but the whole system–be put up, including some self-protection efforts built in.” 13 Options he suggested include having fuel for maneuvers, building resiliency in a system so the loss of one satellite can be overcome, or having back-up laser communications payloads for redundancy since, “We need to protect and defend.” The *Space Safety and Security Strategy* released by Germany in November 2025 calls for “Establishing the capability for comprehensive cyber operations and electromagnetic spectrum operations in the space domain.” 14 (For a longer discussion of the strategy, see Section 8.6, German Counterspace Policy, Doc- trine, and Organization below.)
**8.4 — GERMAN DIRECTED ENERGY WEAPONS** In discussing how to spend the €35 billion on space defense systems that Germany has committed to spend through 2030, Maj. Gen. Michael Traut, commander of the German Space Command, said in February 2026 that one of the technologies could be lasers that could be used to interfere with adversary spacecraft but not create debris in orbit.15 However, laser technology for counterspace purposes was not listed in the options given in Germany’s November 2025 “Space Safety and Security Strategy,” so it is unclear if or how Germany’s work on directed energy weapons would progress. (For a longer discussion of the strategy, see Section 8.6, German Counterspace Policy, Doctrine, and Organization below.)
**8.5 — GERMAN SPACE SITUATIONAL AWARENESS CAPABILITIES** The German Space Situational Awareness Center, known as the Weltraumlagezentrum or GSSAC, has been used by the German Air Force since 2009 to monitor objects in orbit.16 It is a civil-military facility jointly operated by the DLR and the German Space Command, and is managed by the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action and the Federal Ministry of Defence.17 The German Experimental Surveillance and Tracking Radar (GESTRA) tracks objects in LEO and contributes to both Germany’s national catalogue and that of the European Union Space Surveillance and Tracking (EU SST).18 It operates in the microwave range and has been operational since 2024.19 The transmitting and receiving systems are each composed of 256 individual antennae; it is partially mobile and has separate reception and transmission systems.20 The Fraunhofer Institute for High Frequency Physics and Radar Techniques (Fraunhofer FHR), a government-funded research institute, has TIRA (Tracking and Imaging Radar), which can track space objects. It has a tracking radar
08-02

that transmits in the L-band frequency and an imaging radar that transmits in the Ku-band frequency. Its antenna is 34 meters in diameter and can be turned. DLR’s Johannes Kepler Observatory (JKO) has a 1.75 m telescope (Ritchey- Chrétien design) in the Northern Black Forest that is used to detect and track objects in LEO.24 Its calculated visual magnitude limit is ~23.25 Germany and the United States signed a space situational awareness (SSA) sharing agreement in January 2015.26 In 2019, Germany joined the Combined Space Operations (CSpO) initiative to develop coordination and interoperability of space operations, increase resilience, and encourage responsible behavior in outer space.27 Germany and the Spanish company Indra signed a contract in February 2025 for an upgraded version of Indra’s space surveillance S3TSR radar; this purchase is part of Germany’s LEO – Groundbased Upscaled AESA Radar or “L-GUARD” program, which is under its Space Surveillance System.28 This radar will be operated by the German Space Command via remote access from the GSSAC.29 A strategy of maintaining competitiveness and autonomy internationally in the SSA domain is also being pursued by the EU SST, of which Germany is a prominent member. The EU SST increased the budget contracted to European industry in R&D and capabilities by 205% in 2020-2022, compared to the 2018- 2019 budget.30 In February 2024, the European Health and Digital Executive Agency completed a set of grant agreements under the Horizon Europe projects to support research and development for EU SST services.31 The total budget made available by the EU for the five projects is €52 million for the 2023-2025 period.32 In September 2024, the network of sensors contributing to EU SST started growing with the integration of new commercial sensors, resulting from of a public procurement procedure led by the Centre national d’études spatiales (CNES) for the acquisition of commercial data 33 for a total maximum amount of €13.2 million that was launched in 2023.34 The new sensors aim to enhance the provision of the EU SST services, such as collision avoidance, re-entry analysis, and fragmentation analysis).35

**8.6 — GERMAN COUNTERSPACE POLICY, DOCTRINE,** **AND ORGANIZATION** ***Policy and Doctrine*** Germany’s *National Security Strategy*, published in June 2023, talks about the importance of space in regards to national security and daily lives and goes on to state, “The Federal Government will therefore place a stronger focus on space as a strategic dimension and expand its capabilities in this domain.” 36 In discussing partnerships, it says, “Allied defence also encompasses cyberspace and space. Attacks in or from these dimensions can have the magnitude and impact of an armed conflict and thus necessitate collective action. The Federal Government will promote the development and introduction of highly advanced capabilities.” 37 The *German Federal Government’s Space Strategy*, released in September 2023, has a section on “Security, strategic options and global stability.” 38 It says that building off of the *National Security Strategy*, the EU, and NATO provide “the central framework for addressing space security issues” and that “space plays an important role in national security.” 39 It talks about the importance of a rules-based order, noting, “We are calling for use of space to be based on rules, and to be secure.” 40 It brings up that the “intentional destruction of objects in space, in tests of ground-based, destructive anti-satellite weapons, has also added to the debris” and that Germany and its allies have made commitments not to conduct those types of tests.41 The strategy indicates that the German government is going to prioritize “the development and expansion of additional capabilities for space situational awareness.” 42 Germany released its *Defense Policy Guidelines* in November 2023.43 In it, space is described as being of “strategic relevance” and one permanent mission of the German armed forces is “contributing to the national situation picture in space.” 44 As well, it says “the nature of the threat environment,” means that it is “necessary to operate beyond geographically defined areas, namely in the cyber and information domain, and in space.” 45 In September 2025, Brig. Gen. Jürgen Schrödl, of the German Ministry of Defence, stated, “We have to accept that space is a tested domain, is a war- fighting domain, is becoming a war-fighting domain.” 46 At that same conference, Maj. Gen. Michael Traut, commander of the German Space Command, stated that operational capabilities are needed “in and for space,” and that those operational capabilities “consist of defensive and offensive means…I can repeat that officially. Defensive and offensive means, shield and sword.” 47 Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced in September 2025 that Germany plans to spend €35 billion on military space-related projects by 2030, citing threats from Russia and China and the vulnerabilities of satellite networks as justification.48 He also talked about “guardian satellites,” establishing a military satellite operations center inside the German Space Command, strengthening space situational awareness, and hardening systems for their protection.49 Pistorius said that Germany must “discuss offensive capabilities” so that it will “be able to deter in space in order to be defensible.” 50 He pointed out that “Even today, the systems of the German Armed Forces are affected by jamming attacks” and that Russia’s cyberattack on ViaSat in February 2022 had significant effects in Germany as well: “The operational control of a total of almost 6,000 wind turbines was massively restricted.” 51 To contextualize this planned military space spending, €35 billion is comparable to the European Space Agency (ESA)’s five-year budget.
08-04

Germany published its *Space Safety and Security Strategy* in November

2025. The joint foreword by Boris Pistorius, federal minister of defence, and Johann Wadephul, federal minister for foreign affairs, notes, “A central pillar of this strategy is close cooperation with our NATO Allies and our European and international partners. Developing and enforcing norms, rules and principles for the peaceful, responsible and sustainable use of space is only possible if we work together.” 54 The strategy states that “security-relevant space infrastructure and systems are as essential a part of defence-related infrastructure as vital and defence-critical facilities on Earth.” 55 Some of the principles it says that must be prioritized are “Achieving the capability for military space operations” and “Achieving the capability for cyber operations and electromagnetic spectrum operations in the space domain.” 56 Russian and Chinese counterspace activities are cited to demonstrate the threat to the space domain, while SSA and the ability to detect and defend against threats requires “new capabilities to conduct space operations, such as reusable spaceplanes, inspection and surveillance satellites, and on-board sensors for satellites to identify any attempts to approach and interfere.” 57 It asserts that “potential enemies can only be deterred if we have the necessary capabilities, are willing to use them and communicate this willingness;” as such, the strategy says that “we will ensure Germany’s ability to take action in the space domain along the entire spectrum from peace to crisis to national and collective defence.” 58 Some technologies mentioned as those that Germany wants to conduct research in are: active co-orbital protection, on-orbit servicing, “space-based contributions to territorial ballistic missile defence,” and “reusable spaceplanes.” 59 Finally, it calls space “an independent and dynamic area of military operations” and thus “We are strengthening the Bundeswehr’s ability to act in space and enabling it to limit the use of space by adversaries. The operation of space systems, conducting space operations and the ability to generate effects in space are essential military capabilities.” 60 It ends with lists of strategic lines of action, which include:
- “Establishing a classifiable wargaming centre as well as a simulations and space testbed
- “Strengthening the responsibility of the Bundeswehr Space Command in exercising military responsibility over the space domain and improving the necessary command and control processes in accordance with the principle of unity in command
- “Developing technical and operational capabilities to restrict/prevent military use of space by an adversary at national level and/or in cooperation with partners, including deep precision strike and hypersonic capabilities
- “Developing and using highly agile standardised inspection, maintenance and refuelling/logistics satellites as well as reusable spaceplanes to re solve technical problems
- “Developing active and passive protective measures for all space segments, including hardening against electromagnetic pulses and against the impact of nuclear explosions in space
- “Developing and using highly agile low-signal surveillance and bodyguard satellites and reusable spaceplanes to inspect and effect an adversary’s systems
- “Establishing the capability for comprehensive cyber operations and electromagnetic spectrum operations in the space domain” 61

DA-ASAT missile tests, as one of the growing number of signatories to the moratorium on such testing initiated by the United States. In 2024, Germany’s $655 million USD put it in eighth place globally for military space spending.63 Germany has eight military satellites on orbit that are used for remote sensing and communication.64 ***Organization*** The German Space Command was started in July 2021 under the authority of the German Air Force.65 At the time, the Ministry of Defence explained that this was in response to “the increasing significance of space for our state’s ability to function, the prosperity of our population, and the increasing dependency of the armed forces on space-supported data, services and products.” 66 It was stood up at the GSSAC.67 One of the Space Command’s responsibilities is to detect and track objects in space; as well, Defence Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer said at its creation that the goal was to gather all capabilities in one place and to build new ones.68 Kramp-Karrenbauer also said that German space operations “are always defensive operations.” 69 Germany is said to be working on a new military space architecture that will strive to predict what new military space systems are needed and plan out how to ensure they are interoperable, as well as determine when they need to be updated.70 There are three planned phases: the first is intended to be ready in 2029; the second, 2035; and the third is roughly around 2040.71 Germany participates in NATO’s Space Centre of Excellence, which was created in July 2023 and reached full operational status in January 2026.72 According to NATO, the Centre “develops space operations concepts, strengthens staff readiness, supports major exercises, and feeds operational lessons back into NATO’s adaptation cycle.” 73 The US Space Command holds an annual conference, Global Sentinel, to practice combined space operations. The most recent iteration was held in April 2025 and included operators from 29 countries plus NATO; Germany was one of the participating nations.74 According to Maj. Gen. Richard L. Zellmann, Combined Joint Force Space Component deputy commander, the exercises the group worked through ran the gamut from “a normal, standard launch all the way to direct ascent, satellite weapons and everything in between.” 75

The United States started its Schriever Wargame in 1998 as a biennial tabletop exercise to look at how advanced space technologies influenced future conflicts in space. In recent years, the Schriever Wargame has become an annual event that also explored policy and strategy issues, diplomatic, economic, military, and information activities, and included participation from a growing number of allied military and commercial partners. Germany has been participating in it since 2012.76 The 17th and most recent iteration of the Schriever Wargame was held in August 2025, included policy-makers from Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, New Zealand, Norway, and the United Kingdom, and had an Indo-Pacific focus.77 It included a special access cell so that the participants could share information about special access programs.78 The next version of the wargame will be in 2027 and for the first time, will have allies involved in its creation and planning, as opposed to the United States doing all of it.79 Operation Olympic Defender (OOD), USSPACECOM’s plan to protect US and allied satellites during a conflict, was created by USSTRATCOM in 2013 and opened for ally participation in 2018.80 After having rejected in 2021 an offer to join, Germany joined in October 2024.81 The group is working on how to share SSA data in order to develop a common operating picture of space and is now called Multi-National Force-OOD (MNF-OOD).82 **Potential Military Utility /** Germany officials have expressed interest in inspector satellites and spaceplanes and its new *Space Safety and Security Strategy* calls for researching those kinds of capabilities, so it is possible that Germany could have a co-orbital counterspace capability eventually. Germany’s recent acceptance of the Arrow 3 ballistic missile defense system gives it a latent DA-ASAT capability, although it was not designed nor tested for that mission. As well, the preference is to have non-debris-causing ways to interfere with adversary satellites, so this is less likely to be used. German officials’ statements about lasers, combined with its plans to spend €35 billion on space defense systems by the end of the decade, means that DEW could be explored but it would be unlikely to serve any real military utility in the near-term. Based on Germany’s solid existing SSA capabilities and its planned enhancements thereof, it is possible that its SSA capabilities could provide some military utility for both offensive and defensive counterspace operations. Given the policy documents that have come out over the past several years, it does indicate that Germany is looking for an offensive role for its military in space and would consider using counterspace capabilities.

35.6 892°N

# I R AN

51.3890°E

Iran has a nascent space program, building and launching small satellites that have limited capability. Technologically, it is unlikely Iran has the capacity to build on-orbit or direct-ascent anti-satellite (DA-ASAT) capabilities, and little military motivation for doing so at this point. Iran’s military has an independent ability to launch satellites, separate from Iran’s civil space program. Iran has not demonstrated any ability to build homing kinetic kill vehicles, and its ability to build nuclear devices is still constrained. Iran has demonstrated an electronic warfare (EW) capability to persistently interfere with commercial satellite signals and Starlink ground terminals, although its capacity to interfere with military GPS signals is difficult to ascertain.

**9.1 — IRANIAN CO-ORBITAL ASATs** Iran has no known co-orbital ASAT capabilities or development program, and its indigenous satellite manufacturing and operations capabilities are very basic. Iran has put a small number of low-mass satellites on orbit, starting with liquid-fulled SLVs like the Safir and Simorgh, but it has had recent success with mix- and solid-fuelled SLVs built by the Iran Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) like the (respectively) Qassed and Qaem-100. Its pace of launch attempts is slow, possibly due to sanctions on its ability to make progress, or perhaps because it is sensitive to international reaction to satellite launches because of their similarities to ballistic missile launches. Iran has not demonstrated the ability to manufacture satellites with significant on-orbit maneuverability or remote sensing capabilities, nor the ability to successfully conduct precision command-and-control (C2), which would be necessary to develop an effective co-orbital ASAT capability.
**9.2 — IRANIAN DIRECT-ASCENT ASATs** **Assessment /** There is no public evidence that Iran has developed, or is developing, a dedicated DA-ASAT capability. However, Iran does have a robust ballistic missile program, including a demonstrated satellite launch vehicle, which could theoretically be used as a DA-ASAT rocket. It would still need to be combined with several other technologies that Iran has not yet tested. **Specifics /** Iran has several short- and medium-range ballistic missiles, either in operational status or in development, with estimated ranges from 150 km to more than 2,000 km. The longer-range missiles could theoretically be used as the basis for a DA-ASAT rocket, with a potential ceiling of roughly half their ballistic range. There is no evidence Iran has ever tested its ballistic missiles in this role, nor that it has a program to develop this capability. There are some who claim Iran is developing the ability to create crude electromagnetic pulse (EMP) weapons by putting nuclear-tipped ballistic missiles on ships. Such weapons, they argue, could be used to conduct surprise attacks on national power grids, or as an indiscriminate ASAT weapon.1 However, many other experts discount Iran’s ability to use a primitive nuclear device in this way 2 and state that this is a scare tactic designed to promote missile defense.3

09-02

In February 2020, Iran tried to launch the Zafar 1, a communications satellite, via the Simorgh SLV. However, it experienced an anomaly at some point between the second and third stages. Defense Ministry space program spokesperson Ahmad Hosseini stated, “Stage-1 and stage-2 motors of the carrier functioned properly and the satellite was successfully detached from its carrier, but at the end of its path it did not reach the required speed for being put in the orbit.” 17 An unsuccessful space launch was detected by US military analysts in June 2021; it is unclear what rocket was used, but it is possible that it was a Simorgh. A second launch may have been held at that same launch pad later that month, possibly of a Simorgh again.18 In December 2021, Iran launched a Simorgh with three payloads on-board, none of which appear to have made it to orbit.19 A successful launch of the Simorgh SLV finally occurred in January 2024, when a Simorgh lifted three satellites to an altitude of 450 km. The four objects from the launch have only been catalogued as Object A (2024-018A, 58849), Object B (2024-018B, 58850), Object C (2024-018C, 58851), and Object D (2024-018D, 58852) and it is unclear which satellite corresponds to which object. Two cubesats, Kayhan-2 and Hatef-1, are intended to test narrowband communication and geopositioning technology. A larger third satellite, Mehda, is described as a “research satellite” intended to help the ISA ascertain how well the Simorgh is at placing objects in orbit.20 In December 2024, a Simorgh LV was launched from the Imam Khomeini Space Launch Terminal and via a multi-phase mission, took to orbit a domestically designed and manufactured space tug (Saman-1), as well as a nanosat (Fakhr-1 communication satellite) and an unnamed research payload.21 The Saman-1 was designed at the Iranian Space Research Center and is intended to bring satellites to higher orbits to obviate the need for bigger SLVs.22 The launch put its payloads (Iran’s heaviest indigenously-launched payload to date) in an elliptical orbit where the apogee is 410 km and the perigee is 300 km.23 The Aerospace Industries Organization (AIO), a civilian entity, has announced plans to develop three new SLVs. The first is the Sarir, a follow-on to the Simorgh, and is intended to be a liquid-fuel SLV that can take payloads up to 700 kg to 1000 km.24 Then there is the Soroush, which is supposed to use parallel booster rockets to get payloads to geosynchronous orbit, and the Soroush-2, which is intended to use cryogenic fuels to enable payloads up to 2500 kg to reach GEO.25 These are all notional and have yet to appear on any launch pads. ***Military Space Launch Vehicles*** In addition to the civil SLVs being developed by the Iranian Space Agency, the Iranian military is also developing their own SLV that has shown more success. Satellite imagery has detected a limited number of what appear to be engine tests at the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)’s Jihad Self-Sufficiency Organization at the Shahroud facility (see Imagery Appendix, pg. 17-21), and in February 2020, Iranian officials released imagery of a motor being tested there, which they stated was of the Salman engine (intended to be a smaller upper stage motor).26 Footage showed that the developers appear to have been able to make at least two technologies that would be helpful for an SLV program and also a long-range ballistic missile capability: carbon fiber motor casings and thrust vector control (via flexible nozzles).27 The same day that the Salman motor footage was released, Iranian news reported that a solid fueled SLV, the Zuljanah, was finished and would be able to launch the Nahid I satellite, potentially as early as June 2020.
