Footage of the launch of the Zuljanah rocket was aired on Iranian television in February 2021. The launch did not attempt to put a satellite in orbit, but Iranian defense ministry officials who oversaw the program stated that it could carry one 220 kg-sized satellite or 10 smaller ones.29 Satellite imagery in February 2022 showed the aftereffects of an apparent explosion at the Imam Khomeini Spaceport; the damaged gantry resembled the one used for launching the Zuljanah satellite launch vehicle in 2021.30 Reports emerged in June 2022 that Iran had launched the Zuljanah SLV but it is unclear when the launch occurred. Again, the Zuljanah did not appear to be carrying any satellites.31 In April 2020, the IRGC launched from its Shahroud base a satellite (Noor-1, 2020-024A, 45529) on a previously unknown SLV, the Qassed.32 This SLV used a combination of liquid and solid fuel, based respectively on the Iranian Ghadr-110 medium-range ballistic missile and Salman solid-fueled rocket engine. The Qassed has three stages and can be launched via a TEL. Noor-1 was described as a military reconnaissance satellite which appears to be a 6U cubesat; it was detected in an SSO at an altitude of 425 km and it eventually deorbited in April 2022.33 Ali Jafarabadi, head of IRGC’s space force, announced in June 2020 that Iran is working on an all solid-fuel Qassed-2 SLV, which he said is lighter and can carry payloads farther, and indicated an interest in launching something to GEO.34 In July 2025, Iran held a suborbital flight test of the Qassed, which state media described as “assessing some emerging new technologies in the country’s space industry.” 35 In January 2022, the IRGC reported that it launched a solid-fueled rocket for the first time.36 The IRGC successfully launched Noor-2 (2022-024A, 51954) on the Qassed SLV to an altitude of 500 km in March 2022. This marked the second military satellite in orbit for Iran.37 The third military satellite for Iran, Noor-3 (2023-150A, 57962), was launched in September 2023, also on a Qassed SLV; this is thought to be an imaging satellite and has been tracked to an altitude of about 450 km.38 The IRGC successfully launched a new three-stage, solid-fueled SLV called the Qaem-100 in November 2022 in a test flight that was suborbital.39 In January 2024, the IRGC used the Qaem-100 to place the 50-kg Sorayya satellite (2024- 015A, 58817) into an altitude of 750 km, reported to be the highest altitude yet reached by an Iranian satellite.40 The IRGC announced after the Sorayya was launched that it intended to test another new SLV, the Qaem-105, within the next year, and the Qaem-120 within three years; the Qaem-120 is planned to allow Iran to reach GEO.41 In September 2024, the Qaem-100 launched a payload to 550 km altitude: the 60-kg, domestically-developed Chamran-1 (2024-165B, 61072).42 Per Iranian state media, its primary mission is “to test hardware and software systems for orbital maneuvering technology.” It also is intended to “assess the performance of cold gas propulsion subsystems and evaluate navigation and attitude control systems in space.” 43

09-04

In 2010, Iran announced its plans to create a launch base at Chabahar, along its southeastern coast. After many years of work, it appears that the initial design and construction phase may be completed by March 2026. Phase 2, where it can launch international payloads, is to be completed by 2031 and 46 phase 3 - launching solid-fuel LVs-at some point after that. The Chabahar base is intended to be able to launch larger SVs, and it is also relatively near the equator (25 degrees north latitude), which gives it some advantages to launch satellites in certain orbits.47 ***Foreign Launch Vehicles*** Iran does have plans to launch larger satellites, developed both domestically and through bilateral cooperation with other countries.48 So far, Russia has been the foreign launcher of choice, starting in October 2005 with the launch of Sina-1 (2005-043D, 28893), Iran’s first satellite, designed to conduct remote 49 sensing and telecommunications. Russia launched another remote sensing satellite (“Khayyam”, 2022-096A, 53370) for Iran in August 2022. Iranian officials said that the satellite was intended to conduct environmental monitoring and scientific research.50 In 2024, Russia launched Pars-1 (2024-039Q, 59065) in February 2024, while Kowsar (2024-199AL, 61769) and Hodhod (2024-199AK, 61768) (which were reported to have been developed privately) were launched in November.51 In 2025, Russia launched Iran’s Nahid-2 communications satellite (2025-155, 64886) in July as part of a batch with 19 Russian satellites; and in December, Russia launched Iran’s Kowsar, Paya (or Tolou-3), and Zafar-2 satellites.52 All three satellites have imaging sensors, with Paya having propulsion capabilities in order to station keep and, at 150 kg, is Iran’s heaviest Iranian satellite launched to date.53 Russia is also thought to be working on a geostationary communications satellite, “Ekvator;” while it is not clear that Iran is the customer, its slot is 34 degrees east longitude, which according to the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), is a slot that is reserved for an Iranian communication satellite.54

**9.3 — IRANIAN ELECTRONIC WARFARE** **Assessment /** Iran has demonstrated an EW capability to persistently interfere with the broadcast of commercial satellite signals and has interfered with Starlink ground terminals, although its capacity to interfere with military signals is difficult to ascertain. It appears to have received at least two EW jammers from Russia. **Specifics /** Iran has been accused of repeatedly interfering with commercial communications satellites’ ability to broadcast Persian-language programming into Iran over the last several years. In some cases, it appears Iran coordinated with other States to perform the jamming. For example, the jamming of Telstar 12’s broadcast of Persian-language content originating from California was jammed from Havana, Cuba, started in 2003, and eventually, similar jamming occurred from Bulgaria and Libya in 2005/2006.55 Eventually, it appears, Iran became able to jam these channels from within its own territory.

In 2010, the ITU ordered Iran to assist in stopping the jamming originating from its territory, saying that it was acting on two complaints from Eutelsat that its broadcasts of Persian language programs by the BBC and the Voice of America have been interfered with.56 Eutelsat stated in October 2022 that two of its satellites were undergoing jamming from transmissions originating in Iran.57 Iran may have sufficient electronic warfare capability to interfere with satellite- based command and control signals or GPS signals. In late 2011, a stealthy US RQ-170 Sentinel UAV landed in Iran.58 The United States confirmed that a UAV had landed in Iran and asked for its return.59 The UAV was reportedly part of an intelligence operation near the Iran-Afghanistan border and there had been no intent for it to land in Iran. The United States first suggested that the UAV crash-landed because of a technical malfunction and later, because of pilot error. Iran claims that it took command of the UAV and brought it down with little damage. Because these UAVs fly at high altitudes and are stealthy, and the UAV was displayed largely in one piece, it is unlikely that it was shot down. It is also unlikely that Iran took control of the UAV: C2 of such a UAV would typically be done over encrypted military satellite channels that would require extremely sophisticated capabilities to hijack. Some reporting suggests that instead of gaining direct control of the UAV, Iranian electronic warfare specialists used a combination of techniques to bring it down. The attack would have started by interrupting C2 communications with the UAV. Reportedly, under these circumstances, a drone would be programmed to return to its home base. In an interview, an Iranian engineer claims that Iran then faked or spoofed GPS coordinates so that the drone would land in Iran, not at its home base in Afghanistan.60 While the ability to conduct such a spoofing attack on the civil GPS signal has been demonstrated,61 conducting a similar attack on the military GPS signal would be much more challenging because it is encrypted. It is possible that Iran may have found a way to jam the military GPS signal, forcing the UAV to fall back on the civil signal. After the capture of the sophisticated drone, Iran claims it had been able to break into encrypted data on-board the drone, gaining access to sensitive information about the program, but this is difficult to confirm from public sources.62 In August 2019, the US government issued public warnings to commercial shipping about potential Iranian jamming and spoofing of space services.63 The warning cites several incidents of ships reporting GPS interference, bridge-to-bridge communications spoofing, and/or other communications jamming.64 Unnamed US officials told CNN that Iran had placed GPS jammers on Iran-controlled Abu Musa Island near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, but so far they have only affected civilian GPS signals and not US military ships and aircraft. There were reports in March 2020 of “circle spoofing” of GPS devices around the staff college for Iran’s Army, the AJA University of Command and Staff.65 There was another incident of circle spoofing detected by the fitness app Strava around an Iranian government facility in Tehran.66 In September 2023, there were numerous reports of commercial airlines losing their navigation systems when flying in the Middle East, with their GPS information being spoofed so that they thought they were somewhere other than they actually were, causing some to fly off-course. At times, the spoofing sent aircraft up to 80 nautical miles off-course. The source of the spoofing 09-06

was traced to outside of Tehran. In some cases, it was also reported that the planes’ Inertial Reference Systems (IRS), which are supposed to serve as back-ups to GPS, were also corrupted by the spoofing. Some believe that Russia is sharing with Iran EW and GPS-interference lessons learned from its actions in Syria and Ukraine.69 GPS interference reportedly followed Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei as he went on a tour in June 2024, which outsiders thought might have been done to protect him against attacks, particularly following the death of Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi in a helicopter crash in May 2024.70 Neshan, an Iranian navigation app, called it “the most extensive GPS disruption” it had recorded, with users in Tehran reporting their positional data was showing that they were at time “significant distances” from where they actually were.71 The Iranian Army opened an electronic warfare center in eastern Iran in August

2024. The center is called “Jangaal,” which is described as “an abbreviation of two Persian words that mean electronic warfare.” 72

Iran is reported to have received the Krasukha-4 and Murmansk-BN EW jamming systems from Russia. The Murmansk-BN is designed to interfere with High Frequency communications with an estimated range of 5000 - 8000 km; it also can interfere with radio signals, satellite communications, and GPS.78 It is based on six trucks, four of which carry antennas that are 32 meters high.79 As a result of Iran’s 12-day war with Israel in June 2025, Iran jammed GPS over several metropolitan areas in Iran to thwart drone and missile attacks. Deputy Communications Minister Ehsan Chitsaz acknowledged, “Some of the disruptions to the GPS system originate from within the country for military and security purposes.” Domestic and international navigation apps were telling users that they were in different parts of the country and the world and showed wrong maps.80 During that war and for a period after, tankers in the Strait of Hormuz reported GPS jamming (the Maritime Information Cooperation & Awareness, or MICA, Center estimated 970 ships per day experienced this), causing traffic through the Strait to drop by 20 percent as many ships chose to pass through during daylight hours only.81 During protests in January 2026, Starlink users in Iran reported interference with their internet access, with some users undergoing packet losses of 30-80 percent.82 It turned out that the Starlink ground terminals were getting their GPS units spoofed,83 which impaired their ability to connect to Starlink satellites; once users switched their settings so that they were using Starlink’s own internal position estimates and not GPS, this interference dropped.84 As well, SpaceX released a software update to help Starlink avoid interference.85 On the other side, hacktivists were able in January 2026 to insert videos of the exiled Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi and what looked like Iranian forces into several channels of the Iranian state broadcaster, with one graphic that read, “This is a message to the army and security forces…Don’t point your weapons at the people. Join the nation for the freedom of Iran.” 86

**9.4 — IRANIAN SPACE SITUATIONAL AWARENESS CAPABILITIES** Iran is developing some SSA capabilities that in theory could eventually be used to track targets and be used in future counterspace capabilities, but currently appear to be very limited in capability and coverage. In 2013, a center in Delijan (see Imagery Appendix, pg. 17-57) was opened that was intended to provide Iran with space object monitoring capabilities via electro-optical, radar, and radio methods.87 As a member of Asia-Pacific Space Cooperation Organization (APSCO), Iran is part of its Asia Pacific Ground-Based Space Object Observation System (APOSOS) and had a telescope installed in support of that in 2016.88 In 2018, Brigadier General Hossein Salami, the deputy commander of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said that Iran had the ability to monitor satellites in LEO.89
**9.5 — IRANIAN COUNTERSPACE POLICY, DOCTRINE,** **AND ORGANIZATION** The IRGC announced in April 2020 the existence of its Aerospace Force’s Space Command.90 Iranian presidents put a lot of emphasis on Iran’s space program. For example, then-president Ebrahim Raisi chaired a meeting of the Supreme Space Council in 2021, which had not convened in over a decade, where he said that Iran would be able to reach GEO by 2026; as of February 2026, this has not happened.91 The meeting also resulted in a launch schedule going through March 2023 to deal with some of the backlog of Iranian satellites waiting to be launched.92 In February 2023, it was reported that the Raisi administration wished to turn Iran into an exporter of space technology services within a year or the end of the Raisi administration, again, demonstrating the government’s continued interest in enhancing its domestic space capabilities.93 President Masoud Pezeshkian said in February 2025 that “We have worked to continuously strengthen our defense capabilities with the efforts of dedicated, innovative young scientists. This development will continue, and dear Iran will join the ranks of countries conducting extraterrestrial flights, showcasing our nation’s scientific strength.” 94 In an effort to achieve independence from the US-created GPS position, navigation, and timing (PNT) system, Iran was reported in 2016 to have designed and manufactured its own Local Positioning System, “Hoda.” 95 Intended to be carried out in three stages, the first stage was to consist of “15 network stations and two data centers” collecting positional data.96 It is not thought to have full national coverage.97

**Potential Military Utility /** Iran’s current counterspace efforts appear focused on electronic warfare and cyber attacks, and not on destructive counterspace capabilities. Its satellites are very short-lived, and without sophisticated rendezvous and proximity technology or C2 capabilities, it is extremely unlikely Iran could command a co-orbital ASAT to deliberately collide with another satellite with any degree of certainty. The best Iran could hope for would be to increase the possibil- ity of a risk of collision to a degree that might force its adversary to alter the trajectory of their satellite. Iran is not known to possess the technology for a kinetic kill vehicle that would be capable of a DA-ASAT attack. If Iran can pro- duce a working nuclear weapon and miniaturize it, develop a ballistic missile or SLV that can carry it, and mate the two, it would theoretically be possible to conduct a crude EMP attack against LEO satellites. However, it would be extremely difficult to direct such an attack against specific satellites, and most US military satellites are hardened against radiation and EMP effects. Such an attack would also have indiscriminate effects against many other non-military satellites in LEO.98

After the Hamas surprise attack in Southern Israel on October 7, 2023, the amount of jamming activities in the region increased quickly, with a focus on GPS interference and jamming of communications networks. It is hard to distinguish from open sources whether the EW is being conducted by Israel, Hamas, or potentially other actors.10 The GNSS interference was degraded to the point where air traffic into Ben Gurion Airport in Israel had slowed considerably due to flight safety concerns.11 As the war has progressed, the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) stated publicly that it was jamming GPS in the region “in a proactive manner for various operational needs. Citizens should be aware that the disruption can cause various and temporary effects on location-based applications.” 12 Pilots were reportedly warned to not depend on GPS when landing in Israel.13 The GPS interference was reported to be both jamming and spoofing. In March 2024, Lebanon’s Foreign Affairs Minister declared in a statement that, “Lebanon holds Israel internationally responsible for the consequences of any accident or disaster caused by Israel’s deliberate policy of jamming air and ground navigation systems, and deliberately disrupting signal receiving and transmitting devices” and added that Lebanon will file a complaint with the UN Security Council.14 In April 2024, researchers working on the origin of false signals affirmed that spoofing activities against GPS signals were conducted from an Israeli air base, causing the US-operated Global Positioning System to list planes, people, and ships in false locations.15 The same month, disruptions in GPS services were noticed in Jordan and neighboring countries, affecting air traffic management and GPS-enabled applications.16 According to observers, these capabilities have been used for defense against vehicles and systems flying at a very low altitude, and in May 2024, interferences were reported to occur preemptively, in anticipation of potential drone strikes.17 At the 100th Radio Regulations Board (RRB) Meeting of the International Telecommunications Union (ITU) in November 2025, the Board highlighted Addendum 6 to Document RRB25-3/11, which contained a submission from the Administration of Israel.18 Within this submission, the Administration of Israel gave information on its efforts pointed out harmful interference cases to receivers in the RNSS, including their commitment to implement operational safeguards, ensuring that transmissions that interfered with receivers in the RNSS were strictly limited to “situations where there was an imminent and verifiable threat to human life or critical national infrastructure, and in such cases, did not exceed a duration of 15 minutes,” after a July 2025 meeting with Jordan and Egypt.19 Since then, no complaint regarding cases of interference to the RNSS has been reported.

**10.4 — ISRAELI DIRECTED ENERGY WEAPONS** Israel is developing a high-energy laser weapon called “Iron Beam” which is part of its Iron Dome defense system. The Iron Beam is a 100 kw laser that is intended to be used against air-breathing threats.20 It is unclear whether Iron Beam could be used against exo-atmospheric targets for dazzling purpos- es, given it is said to have a range of a few kilometers.21 It should be noted that in December 2024, Rafael chairman Yuval Steinitz explained that larger laser beams suffer increased atmospheric interference when weaponized, air disperses their energy, rendering them ineffective at high altitude or over long ranges.22 In January 2025, Rafael announced having signed a contract with the Israel Ministry of Defense for the expansion of Iron Dome intercep- tor production, including advanced Laser Defense System.23 In March 2025, Defense Minister Israel Katz announced that the Rafael-produced Iron Beam laser air defense system would be operational before the end of 2025; this was after several years’ worth of delays in the program.24 However, in this case, it proved accurate as Iron Beam was declared operational in late 2025 after completing final tests.25 In May 2025, Israel’s Ministry of Defense announced that the Israeli Air Force Aerial Defense Array deployed and operated a high-power laser system prototype. This prototype reportedly successfully intercepted enemy threats and according to Brig. Gen. Yehuda Elmakias, head of the research and development unit at the Israel Ministry of Defense’s Directorate for Defense R&D (DDR&D), this deployment “culminat(ed) in the world’s first successful high-power laser interceptions on the battlefield.” 26
**10.5 — ISRAELI SPACE SITUATIONAL AWARENESS CAPABILITIES** Israel has limited SSA capabilities that are primarily derived from its ELM-2080 Green Pine missile defense radar.27 The system was developed as part of the Arrow missile defense system and is known to have a range of 500-900 km, which could be used to track objects in LEO.28 Versions of the radar have been exported to India (see Indian Space Situational Awareness, Section 4.4), (see South Korean Space Situational Awareness, Section 13.3). The United States and Israel signed an SSA sharing agreement in 2015, but it appears more to have been a way to “streamline the process for USSTRATCOM partners to request specific information gathered by its Joint Space Operations Center;” it is unclear if SSA information is shared in both directions between the United States and Israel.29
**10.6 — ISRAELI COUNTERSPACE POLICY, DOCTRINE,** **AND ORGANIZATION** The Space and Satellite Administration was created within the Israeli Ministry of Defense in the 1980s, while the Israeli Space Agency (ISA) was created in 1983 and operates within its Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST).30 The Israeli government agencies focus on scientific research and development for economic benefit, as well as ensuring Israel’s national security is strengthened. The chair of IAI, Boaz Levy, stated in a May 2023 interview that “Israel is working on space warfare capabilities;” he went on to say, “This is an area in which all the superpowers are investing, and if you ask me if I see it happening – then yes, I see it happening, but I don’t know when it will happen.” IAI is owned by the Israeli government but it is not clear that he was speaking for the

**11.4 — JAPANESE SPACE SITUATIONAL AWARENESS CAPABILITIES** The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) has been the primary source of Japan’s SSA capabilities until recently. JAXA’s Kamisaibara Space Guard Center (see Imagery Appendix, pg. 17-58) has a radar facility that can see up to 10 objects of a diameter of 1 meter or greater to an altitude of 2000 km (or 10 cm objects to 650 km), and the Bisei Space Guard Center (see Imagery Appendix, pg. 17-59) has an optical telescope for SSA tracking to GEO.14 Japan is also developing an SSA analysis system at Tsukuba Space Center. The SAKURA (SsA Key technology Unified Research and Analysis system), located at the Tsukuba Space Center, receives space object information, determines if there will be any conjunctions to Japanese satellites (and issues warnings if there are), predicts reentry, and shares information with the Japanese Ministry of Defense and the CSPoC.15 In March 2022, the Japanese Air Self-Defence Force (ASDF) announced the creation of a new space operations unit with an SSA mission. The unit will operate a satellite that will be launched in FY2026 and ground-based radar that is still being built in the Yamaguchi prefecture.16 As of August 2024, Japan’s plan to launch an SDA satellite in FY2026 remains on schedule.17 The Japanese Defense Ministry has been actively developing space situational awareness (SSA) laser-detecting capabilities and setting up a second space operations unit that will utilize electromagnetic waves to monitor and discern threats to its satellites.18 Additionally, LeoLabs announced in May 2022 it had won a “multimillion” dollar contract to provide SSA data and training to the Japanese ASDF.19 Since 2023, the ASDF Space Operations Group has begun “the full operation of a system to grasp the position and orbit of space objects… and notifies satellite operators of the possibility of approaching objects,” according to the Government of Japan.20 On March 15, 2023, Northrop Grumman signed a partnership within Japanese company IHI to develop “small, highly maneuverable satellites and other solutions” to aid Japanese SSA capabilities and help protect satellites in GEO.21 The SDF SSA system is intended to be tied to the US SSA network, and both hope to be linked to JAXA’s network. The fact sheet for the April 2019 2+2 Dialogue held between US and Japanese officials mentioned the possibility of putting US SSA sensors on Japan’s Quasi-Zenith Satellite System (QZSS) GPS augmentation constellation.22 The USAF’s 2021 budget documents included a request for funding two US SSA payloads on the QZSS that would improve “Geostationary Earth Orbit (GEO) Space Situational Awareness capabilities over the Eurasian theater and facilitates resilient capabilities in the Space Surveillance Network (SSN).” In February 2025, Japan launched a QZSS satellite
11-02

carrying the first USSF SSA payload, and the second QZSS-hosted payload was scheduled to launch in late 2025. The February 2025 launch marked the first bilateral US-Japan space effort focused on national security, according to the US Space Force.25 In December 2025, the second payload launch was cancelled on the launch pad, and a new target launch date has not yet been announced.26

**11.5 — JAPANESE COUNTERSPACE POLICY, DOCTRINE,** **AND ORGANIZATION** Japan historically defined peaceful uses of outer space to be non-military, a definition that was formalized by a 1969 Diet resolution. However, in 2008, the Japanese Diet passed the *Basic Space Law* that allowed space to be used for national security purposes, so long as it would be defensive in nature.27 This was part of a larger shift to incorporating space into national security needs. The Cabinet office created two organizations to help focus on the foundations for space security policy: what is now the National Space Policy Secretariat in July 2012, and the Strategic Headquarters for Space Development in 2015.28 The *2018 National Defense Program Guidelines* stated, “To ensure superiority in use of space at all stages from peacetime to armed contingencies, SDF will also work to strengthen capabilities including mission assurance capability and capability to disrupt opponent’s command, control, communications and information.” 29 The guidelines also discussed how for space and cyber, “establishing international rules and norms has been a security agenda.” 30 The guidelines directed Japan to build a “Multi-Domain Defense Force,” as its defense capability which would bring together “capabilities in all domains including space, cyberspace and electromagnetic spectrum; and is capable of sustained conduct of flexible and strategic activities during all phases from peacetime to armed contingencies.” 31 The SDF would, in cases of armed attack against Japan, be permitted to “block and eliminate the attack by leveraging capabilities in space, cyber and electromagnetic domains.” 32 In June 2020, Japan released its *Outline of the Basic Plan on Space Policy*. This document identifies “ensuring space security” as one of the Basic Space Plan’s goals and focuses on satellites for positioning and maritime domain awareness, cooperation with allies on SSA sharing, becoming involved in international discussions on rules, and focusing on mission assurance.33 In November 2024, Japan’s FY2025 defense space budget request totaled over $1.4 billion, close to the FY2023 and FY2024 requests combined.34 In July 2025, Japan’s Ministry of Defense published the nation’s first guidelines for space domain defense, which outlined plans to protect Japanese satellites, identify attacking entities, address jamming of Japanese satellites, and operate satellites in an autonomous and highly maneuverable manner.35 The guidelines also included plans to strengthen responsive launch, engagement in technical cooperation between the public and private sectors in Japan, and cooperation with allies.36 Japan has also announced steps to reorganize its military space activities. In January 2020, during remarks at the 60th anniversary of the *Treaty of Mutual* *Cooperation and Security Between the United States and Japan*, Prime Minister Shinzo Abe noted the need to make the US-Japan alliance more “robust” and “to make it a pillar for safeguarding peace and security in both outer space and cyberspace.” 37 Abe also announced at a session of the Diet in January 2020 that Japan will “drastically bolster capability and systems in order to secure superiority.” During that speech, he announced that Japan would be establishing a space domain mission unit in April 2020, with the goal of having

it be fully operational by 2022. By 2022, the Space Operations Squadron was established within Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force and was intended to work with both USSPACECOM and JAXA. In April 2021, the Japanese ASDF and USSPACECOM signed an agreement to increase collaboration on space security. Under the agreement, an ASDF officer will receive an assignment in the US Space Command headquarters at Peterson Space Force Base, Colorado.40 By 2022, the Space Operations Group was established as an expansion of the Space Operations Squadron within the ASDF.41 Japan has also announced a plan to change the name of the Air Self-Defense Force to the Air and Space Self-Defense Force (ASSDF) by FY2027 to better represent its interest in strengthening space defense.42 In September 2022, Japan formally pledged not to conduct destructive DA-ASAT missile tests, as one of the growing number of signatories to the moratorium on such testing initiated by the United States.43 Japan released a *National Security Strategy* in December 2022 that would allow it, for the first time, to be able to conduct counterstrike operations using long-range missiles.44 This move is intended to integrate Japan’s air and missile defense systems, and is not intended to be used in its space operations, but does signal a change to Japan’s historically defensive posture. The *National* *Security Strategy* also notes that “Japan will drive forward measures to capitalize on Japan’s overall space-related capabilities in the field of security, such as strengthening cooperation between the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) and the SDF.” 45 In July 2022, Japan participated in Global Sentinel, an annual USSPACECOM-led space security cooperation effort across 25 participating nations. During Global Sentinel, Japan supported a regional multinational space operations center to command and control SSA sensors and responded to scenarios that modeled real-world events.46 At a January 2023 meeting of the US-Japan Security Consultative Committee convened by the US Secretaries of Defense and State and the Japanese Ministers of Defence and Foreign Affairs, the ministers released a statement noting that they considered “attacks to, from, or within space present a clear challenge to the security of the Alliance, and affirmed such attacks, in certain circumstances, could lead to the invocation of Article V of the Japan-US Security Treaty;” invocation of Article V would be made “on a case-by-case basis, and through close consultations between Japan and the United States, as would be the case for any other threat.” 47 Japan participated in subsequent Global Sentinel exercises in 2023,48 2024,49 and 2025 hosted by USSPACECOM.50 In June 2023, Japan released a new *Space Security Initiative* (SSI) that outlines the strategy for responding to space threats over the next decade.51 The document described the changing space security environment and the plan for Japan to increase use of space systems for security on Earth, as well as protecting its own use of space. The latter approach focuses on improving the resilience of space systems, more cooperation with allies and between JAXA and the MOD in enhancing SSA, and helping develop international norms of responsible behavior. The SSI also outlined four priorities to achieve security from space: intelligence collection, missile defense, anti-jamming communication capabilities, and position, navigation, and timing (PNT) services.” 52

11-0 4

**Potential Military Utility /** Japan currently possesses very limited potential counterspace capabilities; if and when it develops co-orbital “guardian” satellites, that could enhance its offensive counterspace capabilities. In the interim, Japan could potentially use its limited SSA capabilities to detect, track, and target a modified SM-3 missile as a DA-ASAT against an adversary satellite in LEO, perhaps with additional tracking assistance and intelligence from the United States. Japan likely possesses the technological foundations to conduct EW against space capabilities, but the military utility and effectiveness of its ability to do so is unknown.

125.8198°E

North Korea has no demonstrated capability to mount kinetic attacks on space assets. North Korea does not appear highly motivated to develop kinetic counterspace assets, though certain capabilities in their ballistic missile program could eventually be evolved for such a purpose. North Korea has exhibited the capability to jam civilian and military GPS signals within a limited geographical area.

**12.1 — NORTH KOREAN CO-ORBITAL ASATs** North Korea currently possesses a rudimentary satellite development and command and control capability, but it has not demonstrated any of the rendezvous and proximity operations necessary for a co-orbital ASAT satellite capability. Due to a lack of detected signals and instability of their platforms, both of its two Kwangmyŏngsŏng satellites are thought to have failed soon after launch. Kwangmyŏngsŏng 3-2 (KMS 3-2, 2012-072A, 39026) was reported to be tumbling on December 17, 2012, five days after launch, and Kwangmyŏngsŏng 4 (KMS 4, 2016-009A) was reported to be tumbling as early as February 9, 2016, only three days after launch. However, despite tumbling, the satellites1 were still following a relatively predictable orbital trajectory and did not pose a collision threat to other space objects. Kwangmyŏngsŏng 4 re-entered the atmosphere on June 9, 2023, and Kwangmyŏngsŏng 3-2 re-entered on September 13, 2023. Although both satellites were announced as remote sensing systems, it is doubtful if they conducted much sensor activity due to their early failures. The North Korean satellite expertise is considered to be rudimentary, with the payloads likely being capable of only producing low resolution imagery at best, and it is doubtful if either of the two satellites would have been militarily useful, even had they not failed prematurely. The Malligyong-1 (2023-179A, 58400) is thought to be able to take at best low-resolution pictures. After2 a May 2023 launch failure, South Korean officials were able to dredge parts of the satellite and its launch rocket and announced that they assessed that the satellite “has no military utility as a reconnaissance satellite.” 3 After the successful launch of Malligyong-1 in November 2023, an observer noted that orbit raising maneuvers were carried out by the Malligyong-1 in February,4 June and September 2024, and in January 2025, with nominal positions 5 6 plotting over the mid-Atlantic, instead of North Korea.7 These changes in Malligyong-1’s orbits indicate the possibility for North Korea to control the spacecraft monitor foreign military and political sites. However, radio trackers do not seem to have detected signals from the spacecraft and observers stated that the satellite seemed to be simply adjusting its position in space, returning to its post-launch orbit, rather than attempting a specific maneuver, noting that the satellite was “much too small” to cause any disruptive action.8 In July 2025, the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA) received an emergency conjunction warning from Malaysia of a Malaysian satellite and a North Korean satellite. The approaching North Korean satellite was approximately 75 meters away from the Malaysian satellite, but North Korean satellite operators managed to avoid a collision by performing an evasive maneuver.9 There is no indication that North Korea’s satellites have any counterspace capability nor is there any indication of intent by North Korea to develop such a capability. Any serious attempt at co-orbital counterspace capabilities would require a sophistication that is beyond North Korea’s current technological capacity.

**12.2 — NORTH KOREAN DIRECT-ASCENT ASATs** **Specifics /** The North Korean ballistic missile program traces its start back to the 1980s with the acquisition of Soviet-era Scud technology. At present, no dedicated ASAT program exists separate from the country’s ballistic missile programs. North Korean systems comprise two primary components: rapidly maturing ground-launched ballistic missile capabilities and the development of some radar systems. North Korea has multiple ballistic missile systems, including intermediate- range ballistic missile (IRBM) and intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) classes, which potentially could be used as the basis for future DA-ASAT capabilities. The first is the Pukguksong family of IRBMs, which include the KN-11 (Pukkuksong-1) and the KN-15 (Pukkuksong-2). The KN-11 is a two-stage solid-fuel SLBM with a purported range of 500-2,500 km, while the KN-15 is the land-based variant. North Korea conducted a successful cold-launched test of the KN-15 in May 2017.10 The Hwasong-10 (Musudan) is an IRBM reportedly modeled off of the Soviet R-27/SS-N-6 missile system. The system is liquid-fueled with a maximum range of 3,500 km. The Musudan has a spotty testing record, but the sixth test of the system reportedly was a success.11 The Hwasong-12 (KN-17) is a newer ballistic missile, tested May 14, 2017, August 28, 2017, and September 14, 2017, using liquid propellant and a high-thrust engine and mounted on a transporter erector launcher (TEL). An additional, possibly ICBM-relevant flight test, using a similar engine to the KN-17, was conducted in March 2017. This was possibly just a larger variant of the existing Hwasong-10 IRBM, but the test indicates the ability to comfortably overshoot Guam and reach lower satellite orbital altitudes. The Hwasong-12 is presumed to be a one-stage missile with a range of 3,700-4,500 km.12 North Korean leader Kim Jong Un announced in the annual 2017 New Year’s Address that the country was nearly ready to flight-test an ICBM.13 There were then two ICBM tests in 2017 of a relatively new system, the Hwasong-14. North Korea tested the Hwasong-14 (KN-20) on July 4, 2017, and July 28, 2017, using a lofted trajectory. Several estimates place the range around 10,000 km, placing US cities and satellites beyond LEO potentially at risk.14 The Hwasong-14 is a two- stage liquid fuel design. The Hwasong-15 (KN-22) was launched for the first time on November 29, 2017, when the liquid-fueled ICBM flew on a lofted trajectory to an altitude of 4,500 km.15 If flown on a standard trajectory, it could have a feasible reach of 13,000 km, which, according to David Wright of the Union of Concerned Scientists, “is significantly longer than North Korea’s previous long-range tests.” 16 According to North Korea’s Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), this flight test was of “an intercontinental ballistic rocket tipped with super-large heavy warhead” which could reach “the whole mainland of the US.” 17 There was another launch of an ICBM-class launch vehicle in March 2022; this rocket (either the Hwasong-15 or possibly the newer Hwasong-17) flew a distance of 1100 km and reached an altitude of 6000 km (placing objects in LEO within reach).18 A Hwasong-17 is suspected to have been launched in November 2022; it failed during its flight test.19 North Korean officials announced that they had launched a Hwasong-15 in February 2023; it flew a heavily lofted flight and reached a distance of nearly 1000 km at an altitude of about nearly 5800 km. If it had flown a less lofted trajectory, it is thought that it could reach the continental United States, indicating it could likely reach objects in LEO as well. The Hwasong-17, a liquid-
12-02

fuelled mobile ICBM, was successfully launched in March 2023, at a range of about 1000 km and an altitude of about 6000 km. Three launches of the Hwasong-18, which is also described as ICBM-class and uses solid propellant, were held in 2023: it had a test flight in April 2023; 23 it flew a second time in July 2023, when it ranged about 1000 km and went to an altitude of about 6000 km;24 and then flew a third time in December 2023, when it again ranged about 1000 km and went to an altitude of about 6000 km.25 In October 2024, the launch of a Hwasong-19 missile reportedly covered approximately 1,000 km, reaching an altitude of over 7,000 km before landing in the sea,26 representing, according to Khaled Khiari, Assistant Secretary-General for Asia at the UN Department of Political Affairs, “a grave threat to regional stability.” 27 According to officials in Tokyo and Seoul, this test appeared to be a new type of solid-fuel ICBM.28 North Korea has other presumed ICBM-range systems that have not yet been flight-tested or deployed. The first is the Hwasong-13 (KN-08), a three-stage road-mobile ICBM first seen in the 2012 military parade, and the second is a variant of this missile known as the KN-14, shortened to two stages. These are alleged road-mobile ICBMs displayed in past military parades but have not yet been flight-tested or deployed.29 North Korea’s only known operational space launch vehicle is the Unha-3. It appears to derive design components from the Taepodong-2 (TD-2), which was originally believed by US intelligence to be a possible ICBM.30 Although operational, the reliability of the Unha-3 is not assured. The TD-2 failed in several tests throughout the 2000s, raising some questions regarding both its relationship to the Unha-3 and the latter’s reliability. The first attempt to use the Unha-3 to launch the Kwangmyŏngsŏng 3 satellite in April 2012 resulted in failure, but in December 2012, the Unha-3 successfully placed the first North Korean satellite, Kwangmyŏngsŏng 3-2 in orbit.31 The Unha-3 was used to put the second satellite, Kwangmyŏngsŏng 4 into orbit in 2016.32 Commercial imagery captured in March 2019 of North Korea’s Sohae Satellite Launching Station (see Imagery Appendix, pg. 17-24) indicated that it may have returned to normal operations.33

The Unha-3 is known to be a multi-stage rocket with liquid propellant requiring a conventional launch pad and extensive visible preparations. The first stage consists of four Nodong engines, making it too large for mobile use.35 North Korea’s second proven space launch vehicle is the Chollima-1. North Korean news agency KCNA announced in May 2023 that it had tried to use the Chollima-1 to launch its military reconnaissance Malligyong-1 satellite, but failed in the second stage.36 It was followed up by another attempt in August 2023, with the Chollima-1 again attempting to place the Malligyong-1 in orbit; this time, it failed in its third stage.37 The third attempt for the Chollima-1 proved to be a success. In November 2023, North Korean officials announced the successful launch of the SLV and the placement of the Malligyong-1 into a 512 km by 493 km at 97.43 degrees orbit.38 North Korea reported that Malligyong-1 was an active remote sensing satellite and had imaged US military bases, but there was debate about its functionality until it maneuvered in a series of steps to raise its perigee in mid February 2024.39 In May 2024, North Korea announced that its attempt to launch a new military reconnaissance satellite failed due to an explosion of a newly developed rocket engine during flight.40 Analysts interpreted this attempt to launch a satellite as the potential test of a new form of rocket technology, including the development of a liquid fuel rocket motor.41 According to the vice general director of the National Aerospace Technology Administration (NATA), experts consider that the accident occurred due to the air blast of the new-type satellite carrier rocket during the first-stage flight and is attributable to the reliability of operation of the newly developed liquid oxygen and petroleum engine.42 Moreover, South Korea’s Yonhap News Agency reported that a “large number of Russian experts” had entered North Korea to assist with the launch.43

12-04

Some have speculated that North Korea could combine a ballistic missile and a nuclear warhead into an EMP weapon, targeted against either US satellites or domestic infrastructure. However, it seems unlikely at this point that North Korea would dedicate one of its limited nuclear warheads to an unproven task.44 Although North Korea likely demonstrated a thermonuclear capability in September 2017, it is unknown how large of a yield from a nuclear warhead is necessary to affect the US electrical grid.45 Additionally, North Korea’s ICBM force, while growing in technical sophistication and performance, is not currently capable of carrying such a heavy warhead. Historical nuclear tests in space, such as the US Starfish Prime test in 1962, are known to have generated effects that damaged or destroyed satellites in orbit at the time.46 It would be difficult to predict the ability of creating such effects against military satellites, particularly since many US military satellites are hardened against radiation and EMP effects. Non-hardened satellites would be affected by an EMP, however. For a longer discussion of this, please see Section 2.4, Russian Directed Energy Weapons.

**12.3 — NORTH KOREAN ELECTRONIC WARFARE** On numerous occasions, North Korea has demonstrated the capability to interfere with civilian GPS navigation used by passenger aircraft, automobile, and ship systems in the vicinity of the South-North border and nearby coastal areas.47 This type of interference (i.e., downlink jamming) targets GPS receivers within range of the source of the jamming signal but has no impact on the GPS satellites themselves nor the service provided to users outside the range of the jammers. The area affected will depend on the power emitted by the jammer and the local topography. In the case of the reported North Korean incidents, the range was estimated to be several tens of kilometers. According to unnamed US officials, this type of jamming would not affect US military members who use the military GPS signals.48 The GPS interference incidents along the South-North border appear to have been deliberately targeting civilian receivers, presumably as part of a North Korean political strategy or tactic. Some events have coincided with joint South Korea-US military exercises. North Korea could also be developing jammers that are effective against the military GPS signals, but to date, there is no public evidence of such development, testing, or use. There is extremely limited public information about whether North Korea could jam satellite communications. North Korea does routinely jam terrestrial broadcasts from foreign sources, such as the BBC, Voice of America, Radio Free Asia, and South Korea’s KBS, to prevent their citizens from listening.49 However, there is only one report from 2012 about North Korea possibly jamming military communications being broadcast from a South Korean satellite.50 It is assessed that uplink jamming of communication satellites has otherwise not or has rarely occurred, since that would likely have been reported by the targeted satellite operators. Downlink jamming, which affects only the receivers in a local area, may be occurring within North Korea, but there is no publicly-available information available on this subject. In March 2024, North Korea attempted to jam GPS signals during South Korean military exercises, which marked the first reported use of GPS jamming by North Korea in eight years.51 In May 2024, South Korea reported that 201 airplanes and 731 ships had experienced GPS problems over its national territory and that it had identified the Gangryong and Ongjin regions of North Korea as the source of interference. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lim Soo-suk said that South Korea raised its renewed concerns over this repeated GPS jamming with the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and the International Maritime Organization (IMO).53 In November 2024, South Korean military officials affirmed that North Korea staged GPS interference two days in the North’s Haeju and Kaesong areas, impacting ships and civilian aircraft in South Korea.54 This interference has been interpreted as a way for North Korea “to shield their own communications and intelligence exchanges during critical military operations” both at home and abroad.55 Also in November 2024, a South Korean military reconnaissance drone reportedly crashed due to GPS interference by North Korea. In January 2025, South Korea’s defense ministry reported that North Korea’s GPS jamming had persisted for over three months.56 In October 2025, the ICAO passed a resolution determining that the GNSS interference originating in North Korea was indeed an infraction of the 1944 Convention on International Civil Aviation, condemned it for doing so, and called for it to fulfill its obligations under the Convention.57

**12.4 — NORTH KOREAN SPACE SITUATIONAL AWARENESS CAPABILITIES** There is little publicly available information about North Korea’s SSA capabilities. North Korea does have a General Satellite Control Building, which headquarters its National Aerospace Development Administration (NADA) and is the facility from which North Korea tracks and monitors its own satellite launches.58 Since May 2017, imagery has detected construction on an adjacent facility. The facility is most likely intended to be a space environment test center and most likely does not have SSA capabilities.59 North Korea has been reported to possess Iranian phased array radars as part of its air defense network; their capabilities are unknown.60
12-06

**12.5 — NORTH KOREAN COUNTERSPACE POLICY, DOCTRINE,** **AND ORGANIZATION** There is an absence of discussion on counterspace weapons in the North Korean state media. Surveying the archives from 2010-2025 does not reveal a mention of ASAT or counterspace.61 North Korean state media claimed in April 2020 that “The purpose of the republic’s space development is to adhere to the interests of the state and to use science and technology to solve scientific and technological problems essential to economic construction and people’s lives.” 62 In 2021, however, North Korea publicly expressed an intention to develop space capabilities and achieve “mastery of space defense science and technology” at both the 8th Congress of the Workers’ Party of Korea and the 4th Plenary Meeting of the 8th Central Committee.63 In 2022, North Korea reportedly revised its Space Development Law to allow for the use of space for national defense purposes. The revision removed sentences that committed to only use space for peaceful purposes and that voiced opposition to the “militarization of space,” while introducing the threat of “appropriate countermeasures” in response to countries that attempt to target the North Korean space program.64 The revised Space Development Law also tasked North Korea’s NATA with “the promotion of space development projects to strengthen national defensive capabilities.” 65 In November 2021, the North Korean aerospace sector facilitated a space conference to discuss peaceful space development plans and the use of satellite technology for economic growth. The conference occurred after Kim Jong Un ordered the development of military reconnaissance satellites earlier in 2021, demonstrating a potential increase in desire to develop space assets and technology.66 Kim Jong Un visited the Sohae Launch Center in March 2022 and called for it to be “modernized” so to “enable large carrier rockets to be launched there,” 67 which indicates that SLV capabilities continue to be an increased priority for the North Korean government. Satellite imagery taken later in 2022 indicated that construction is in full swing at Sohae, presumably to carry out the modernization called for by Kim.68
Most state media references to space cite North Korean efforts to successfully launch sat ellites, ostensibly for Earth observation purpos-- es. These references discuss the development of high-thrust engines (usually referenced as the March 18th engine) for delivery of satellites into orbit, and the development of the earth observation satellite technology (only EO sat ellites so far (Kwangmyongsong-4), launched-in 2016). See: “Kim Jong Un Watches Ground Jet Test of Newly Developed High-Thrust Engine,” *Korean Central News Agency*, March 19,

2017. Thus far, official statements from North Korea have emphasized space as a common good: “Space is wealth common to man,” and have emphasized peaceful uses. “Peaceful Development and Use of Space Are Legitimate Right of Sovereign State: DPRK Delegation,” *Rodong Sinmun*, June 21, 2017. State media also references work on meteorological atmospher ic observation systems, which may have some-applications for radar tracking systems. See: “A Breakthrough,” *Naenara News*, July 12, 2015.

In March 2024, observers noted progress in the expansion and modernization of the Sohae complex and, after a period of little activity, signs of advance preparations with personnel on site and the addition of new buildings. A construction site appeared in proximity to the launchpad that was used for the successful launch of the Chollima-1 rocket in November 2023.70 During a briefing in April 2024, Republic of Korea Joint Chiefs of Staff spokesperson, Lee Sung-jun, stated that the “preparations for additional reconnaissance satellite launches by the North Korean military have been continuously detected, but there are no signs of an imminent [launch].” 71 In September 2024, observers reported a construction project at the Thaesong Machine Factory, which likely houses liquid-fuel engine production lines for ICBM or satellite carrier rockets.72 The expansion of the factory reportedly slowed down between the end of 2024 and the beginning of 2025,73 which was interpreted by General Gregory Guillot, head of US Northern Command and North American Aerospace Defense Command, in Congressional testimony as evidence that North Korea “is eager to transition [its] strategic weapons program from research and development to serial production and fielding.” 74 In June 2025, satellite imagery from Planet confirmed on-going construction at Thaesong.75 Imagery analysis highlighted a new annex likely related to TEL and missile testing, ongoing construction of a new factory hall, and the groundwork for a new construction project on the site of former factory halls.76 In July 2025, satellite imagery taken over the Sohae complex revealed that a new maritime pier had been constructed at the launch center.77 The new pier would enable transport of larger rocket components than previously possible using rail, according to an ICEYE representative.78 Imagery revealed a newly constructed jetty and vessels, which indicates potential operational status.79 Additionally, expansion work on road and rail infrastructure throughout Sohae was ongoing as of July 2025.80 **Potential Military Utility /** North Korea likely possesses very limited counterspace capabilities. It lacks significant SSA capabilities, demonstrated hit-to-kill capabilities, or any real RPO capabilities, and has very limited space launch capabilities. This very likely limits North Korean counterspace options to either jamming/spoofing or broad area attacks such as nuclear detonations in LEO that could damage large numbers of satellites over a long period of time.

**13.2 — SOUTH KOREAN ELECTRONIC WARFARE** As part of its Space Odyssey 2050 program, the ROKAF is working on EW counterspace capabilities that can be used to deter or counter adversary space capabilities.11 Few public details are known about the state of development or planned capabilities for this system.
**13.3 — SOUTH KOREAN SPACE SITUATIONAL AWARENESS CAPABILITIES** South Korea is working to enhance its indigenous SSA capabilities through the development of a national SSA infrastructure planned to be operational by the mid-2020s. It was anticipated to include a space weather forecast system, reconnaissance satellites, and an electro-optical satellite surveillance system. In August 2021, military officials from South Korea and the United States agreed to cooperate on security space issues. Signed between Gen. Park In-ho, the ROKAF chief of staff, and General Raymond, USSF chief of space operations, it established a joint consultative body on space policy. They also agreed to share information on SSA, hold joint drills, and work to enhance joint space operations capabilities. ROKAF Colonel Park Ki-tae, chief of the Korean Space Operations Center (KSpOC), indicated SSA is a priority for the ROKAF, stating in October 2021 that “What we urgently need is ‘eyes’ to look at what’s happening in outer space.” The bilateral Space Cooperation Working Group that met in Washington, DC, in April 2022 resulted in another signed agreement on cooperation on space security issues, including sharing SSA data, and the creation of a joint space policy research organization. As a result of bilateral agreements between the United States and South Korea, the United States has launched a series of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites for South Korea. The first satellite launch from the Vandenberg Space Force Base in California took place in late 2023, followed by two more satellite launches in 2024. In April 2025, South Korea’s *Yonhap* news agency announced the successful launch of the fourth satellite. In November 2025, South Korea’s fifth and final reconnaissance satellite was launched by the United States, marking a completion of the space-based surveillance network.18 In February 2023, South Korea delivered a statement at the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) Scientific and Technical Subcommittee (STSC), declaring that the Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute, serving as the national SSA agency, operates an electronic optical monitoring system, the Optical Wide-field patroL Network (OWL-Net) for tracking objects in low Earth orbits below 2,000 km, alongside a Satellite Laser Ranging (SLR) system for monitoring specific targets.19 South Korea also revealed a project to introduce an optical monitoring system for space objects in the areas of 2,000 to 36,000 km, and the development of a SSA radar system to monitor space objects with a diameter of 10 cm or more in LEO.20 In another statement in January 2024, South Korea stated that a telescope will be developed and deployed in the southern hemisphere to complement the OWL-Net space object optical surveillance system currently operating in the northern hemisphere to monitor objects located in MEO and GEO.21 In February 2025, in a technical presentation to the COPUOS Scientific and Technical Subcommittee, South Korea gave a precise description of their OWL-Net global SSA system, stating that the network is composed of five robotic observatories located in Mongolia (OWL-1), Morocco (OWL-2), Israel (OWL-3), United States (OWL-4), and South Korea (OWL-5 and OWL-6), including a domestic SSA system using precise orbit determination through laser ranging measurement and optical observation.
13-02

South Korea declared that in 2023, they started the Project Korea Enhanced Platform for Lowering spacE Risk (KEPLER), an integrated system designed to assess risks related to space object reentry and collisions using data from optics, radar, and lasers.23 In 2025, presenting the architecture of the KEPLER project to the COPUOS Scientific and Technical Subcommittee, South Korea representative unveiled a database spacebook to observe, collect, analyze and manage data, complemented by a Space Risk Warning Portal to display and distribute data to users.24

**13.4 — SOUTH KOREAN COUNTERSPACE POLICY, DOCTRINE,** **AND ORGANIZATION** ***Policy*** In 2013, the ROKAF unveiled its “Space Odyssey 2050,” a three-part strategy that aims to build its own space capabilities by 2050 to protect South Korea’s military forces. As part of the strategy, the ROKAF plans to develop the ability to monitor and “counter” space threats.25 In October 2022, South Korea formally pledged not to conduct destructive DA- ASAT missile tests, as one of the growing number of signatories to the moratori- um on such testing initiated by the United States.26 ***Organization and Budget*** The ROKAF launched its KSpOC in September 2021, which is charged with creating and carrying out space policy, as well as working with other branches of the South Korean government on enhancing space capabilities.27 It will have three departments: one for sharing space information, one for space policy development, and one for developing space weapons. According to ROKAF Chief of Staff Gen. Park In-ho, “The Air Force’s space center will focus its capabilities on developing our national defense space force through building space weaponry, training professionals, and strengthening the organization. That will strengthen our national security in space and enable the Air Force to become a space force.” 28 In December 2022, the ROKAF established a Space Operations Squadron. Major Kim Jong-ha, commander of the newly created ROKAF’s Space Operations Squadron, declared that the squadron comprises five divisions, including the KSpOC, Space Surveillance Team and Satellite Control Team, and “is tasked with informing the entire military of space threats and the common operational picture (COP) to help each military branch to operate its plan effectively,” while working in cooperation with the US Space Force.29 South Korean officials announced that they intended to spend $619 million on space programs in 2022, a 15% increase from 2021 levels; of this, $175.8 million was slated for SLV development.30 $70 million was intended to be spent on developing the Korea Positioning System, South Korea’s planned PNT constellation of eight satellites to be deployed between 2027 and
2034. In March 2023, South Korea announced another significant increase in spending on space programs of $674 million, an increase of 19.5% from
2022.31 The second largest item in the budget ($113.6 million) is for development of a next-generation space launch vehicle, and the third largest item ($73.1 million) is for space defense programs.32 After the adoption of a special law in January 2024, South Korea created the Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA), with a budget of 758.9 billion won ($556 million). an amendment to the Space Development Promotion Plan, with various missions, including space security. Under legislative revisions, South Korea is also considering the establishment of a National Space Security Center, under the National Intelligence Service, that could respond to threats faced by space infrastructure and other enemy threats in the space domain.35 In June 2024, South Korean government agencies and research institutions started working on secure satellite systems, with the formation of a consultative body of twenty organizations, dedicated to protecting satellites throughout their entire life cycle. Including government agencies, the military, and research institutions, the goal of the consultative body is to help counter potential cyber threats against satellite systems.36 Moreover, the National Intelligence Service can now establish and enforce security guidelines related to data on space assets.37 In July 2025, South Korea’s Defense Acquisition Program Administration (DAPA), Korea Aerospace Administration (KASA), and the Korea Coast Guard announced a jointly-led project to launch 30 ultrasmall satellites by 2030, designed to monitor activity in North Korea. This satellite constellation falls within a broader effort to streamline management and regulation of joint civil-military space development projects.38 ***Doctrine*** In July 2022, South Korea participated in Global Sentinel, a USSPACECOM-led space security cooperation effort across 25 participating nations. During Global Sentinel, South Korea supported a regional multinational space operations center to command and control SSA sensors and responded to scenarios that modeled real-world events.39 In April 2023, South Korea announced plans to hold a table-top exercise with military and government officials to examine how to respond to dangers from space and strengthen coordination between the military and space-related agencies.40 Defense officials declared that the exercise will be held once a year.41 In January 2025, at Osan Air Base, South Korea, US Space Forces Korea held the first phase of Polaris Hammer – Korea, a space warfighter inclusive command-and-control exercise designed as a three-stage exercise in coordination with the US Space Force 392nd Combat Training Squadron.42 According to Colonel John Patrick, SPACEFOR-KOR commander, “[this] event was the first time US Space Forces Korea, with six [US Space Force] and South Korean command organizations, executed an operational level combined and joint command and control exercise.” Phase II of Polaris Hammer – Korea was scheduled to occur in conjunction with combined exercise Freedom Shield 25, held by the United States and South Korea in March 2025.43 It is unknown when the third phase of this exercise will be held. In February 2025, senior leaders from US Space Force’s Space Operations Command met with Lieutenant General Kim Hyoung Soo, commander of the ROKAF Operations Command, and toured South Korea’s Space Operations Group to discuss integration at the operational level and strategic level of war between the United States and South Korea.44 In September 2025, DAPA signed an agreement with France’s procurement agency, committing to expand research, development, and intelligence sharing in the defense space sector and to facilitate an exchange of experts between South Korea and France.45

13-04

**Potential Military Utility /** In theory, South Korea’s indigenously-developed space launch and ballistic missile expertise could be leveraged for a future DA-ASAT capability. However, given that South Korea has not tested additional technologies, such as hit-to-kill intercept, it is unlikely to be very capable. Also, since South Korea does not have an indigenous SSA capability yet, its ability to target objects in orbit is questionable; however, it does intend to develop its SSA capabilities within the middle of the decade and it has signed an SSA-sharing agreement with the United States, so it is possible that this could change. The ROKAF may have a basic EW counterspace capability through its Space Odyssey 2050 program, although again this is in very early stages (if it does indeed exist anywhere outside a planning document).

**14.2 — UNITED KINGDOM SPACE SITUATIONAL AWARENESS** **CAPABILITIES** RAF Fylingdales (see Imagery Appendix, pg. 17-32) has been the site of an operational radar since 1963, providing ballistic missile early warning to the US and UK governments.8 Furthermore, as part of its participation in the Space Surveillance Network, its solid-state phased array radar can track objects to an altitude of 3000 nautical miles.9 UK space surveillance technology is being incorporated into the European Space Agency (ESA)’s first coordinated tracking campaign by contributing, via the UK Space Agency (UKSA), the capabilities of the Chilbolton Observatory (a meteorological radar experimental facility) and Space Insight’s Starbrook (an optical space surveillance sensor system).10 The Chilbolton Advanced Meteorological Radar (CAMRa) can detect objects with a radar cross section as small as 1 square meter as far as 1000 km in altitude, while the Starbrook sensor can detect objects down to 1 meter as far as 40,000 km in altitude.11 In April 2023, the United Kingdom asked industry to propose bids for a new ground-based telescope located at a UK military base in Cyprus.12 In November 2023, the UK Ministry of Defence announced that SpaceFlux has been tasked with establishing and operating the telescope in Cyprus, named Project Nyx Alpha.13 There have been no public updates to this project as of February 2026. The United Kingdom and the United States signed an SSA data sharing agreement in September 2014.14 In early 2022, the UKSA announced a pilot program called “Monitor Your Satellites,” a service where operators of UK-based satellites could receive warnings of close approaches between their satellites and other space objects. While it was invite-only at the beginning, the service was eventually opened up to all UK operators and by October 2022, one-third of all UK satellite operators
14-02

had signed up for the service. In a 2022-2023 Annual Report compiled by the UKSA, “Monitor Your Satellites” was then being used by the operators of over 70 percent of UK satellites. The UK National Space Operations Centre was tasked to take over “Monitor Your Satellites” by April 2024.17 The UK Space Command released the *Cross-Government Space Domain* *Awareness Requirements* in August 2024.18 This initiative aimed to develop system of systems SSA requirements and to “inform industry and academia about potential future needs within the government space sector.” 19 ***Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability (DARC) Program*** In December 2023, the United States announced that Australia and the United Kingdom had officially joined the Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability (DARC) program.20 DARC is an effort to develop a new set of radars to detect, track, and identify objects in deep space and consists of three geographically distributed sites that each have multiple transmit and receive radars meshed together (see US Space Situational Awareness Capabilities, Section 1.5). The United Kingdom announced plans to build 27 radar dishes for the DARC program, which will be located in Pembrokeshire in southwest Wales. In June 2024, Pembrokeshire locals launched an opposition campaign to the planned project, which they claimed would impact the landscape that attracts tourism to the area.21 In August 2024, however, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) stated that the DARC program is crucial for allied efforts to monitor threats in deep space, and UK press reporting confirmed that the radar site will continue as planned.22 Northrop Grumman was awarded the DARC radar site contract for the United Kingdom, “Site 2,” in September 2024.23 DARC has been having issues maintaining its set schedule. USSF’s Gen. Stephen Purdy said in February 2025 that DARC might be one of the “slow” and “expensive” legacy systems that might be better replaced by commercial providers.24 A June 2025 report by the US Government Accountability Office (GAO) noted that delays in the build of Site 1 because of issues in creating the site’s systems integration lab were “due to the contractor’s lack of expertise in building such a lab” and that seven-month delay had created follow-on delays.25 For example, “the program delayed Site 2 construction by 9 months to April 2027 and deferred operational acceptance by 13 months to November

2029. Similarly, for Site 3, the program postponed both construction start and operational acceptance by 26 months, to September 2029 and January 2032, respectively.” 26 In August 2025, Northrop Grumman reported that Site 1’s “calibrated antenna arrays operated as a single system to successfully characterize the movement of multiple satellites and demonstrate the effectiveness of the system’s precision radar tracking technology” and is scheduled to be completed in 2027.27 The growing cost of construction for Site 1 could impact the future of program funding for Site 2 as well, yet the overall project is still scheduled to be operational by 2032.28
